Akiba.def: The cult of the fire-quelling deity of Akiba, whose small neighborhood shrines were the most widely spread in Japan - often built of stone, because stone does not burn.

Bidens tripartita.def: Three-lobe beggarticks: an annual of wet waste ground, among the first plants back on an abandoned paddy.

Bon.def: The midsummer festival of the returning dead, when a household visits and tends its grave.

Buyi.def: One of the ethnic minorities of Guizhou in southwest China, whose villages keep fengshui forests.

Calamagrostis.def: Small-reed: the coarse grass of the wet meadow on the higher, less-flooded ground above the sedge marsh.

Carex.def: Sedge: the tufted grass-like plants of the wet meadow between reed swamp and dry ground.

Castanopsis.def: Chinquapin: the evergreen broadleaf of the East Asian hill wood, the stand type the density figures are taken from.

DBH.def: Diameter at breast height: the thickness of a tree's trunk measured at chest height, the size at which a survey counts a stem.

EUNIS.def: The European habitat classification, which names the layers of a woodland edge.

Echinochloa crus-galli.def: Barnyard grass: the coarse annual weed of wet ground, first to take an abandoned paddy.

Edo period.def: The two and a half centuries of the shogunate's rule, 1603-1868, from which most of the record's Japanese evidence comes.

FAO.def: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, whose irrigation training manuals the record cites.

Five Dynasties.def: 907 to 960: the broken half-century between the Tang and the Song.

Fortune.def: One of the setting's lesser deities. Two are a Great Clan's patrons and take its sovereign temples.

GIS.def: Mapping software that measures an area from a boundary drawn on a map.

GSI.def: The Geospatial Information Authority of Japan, the national mapping agency, whose topographic legend gives a bamboo grove its own symbol.

Genroku.def: The Genroku era, 1688-1704, the height of Edo prosperity and the date on many of the village registers the record reads.

Hakone barrier.def: The barrier station on the Tokaido at Hakone, the most famous of the highway checkpoints where travelers and their goods were inspected.

Han dynasty.def: The Han, 206 BC to AD 220, whose tomb models are much of what is known of the ordinary Chinese farmyard - the pigsty-latrine among them.

Heian.def: The Heian period, 794-1185, when the court at Kyoto ruled Japan.

Hyōjōsho.def: The shogunate's supreme judicial council, which sat outside Edo castle.

IRRI.def: The International Rice Research Institute, in the Philippines, whose modern paddy-water and drying figures the record reads backward from.

Important Cultural Landscape.def: A national designation in Japan given to a whole area rather than to one building; Harie's spring water was selected as one together with the neighboring Shimofuri district.

Inari.def: The rice deity, whose small fox-guarded shrine most compounds and villages kept.

Jodo.def: The Pure Land school of Japanese Buddhism, the largest parish network of the Edo period.

Jodo Shinshu.def: The True Pure Land school of Japanese Buddhism, whose temple priests could marry and pass the temple to a son.

Kamakura period.def: The Kamakura period, 1185 to 1333, the age of the first warrior government - earlier than the Muromachi and Edo periods the record mostly draws on.

Kannon.def: The bodhisattva of compassion; an image of Kannon commonly stands over a grave mound or beside a memorial stupa.

Kaogongji.def: The classical Chinese text that lays down the ideal capital: a square wall, three gates a side, nine crossing streets, the palace at the center.

Keicho.def: The Japanese era 1596 to 1615, at the founding of the shogunate.

Kishu school.def: The Kishu school of Edo-period Japanese hydraulic engineering, whose works - Minuma-dai, 1728 - are the record's exemplar of a head canal deliberately divided into two.

Kofun period.def: The tomb-mound period of Japan, roughly the third to the sixth century, before the Nara court - the age of the oldest irrigation works of western Japan.

Kyoho.def: The Kyoho era, 1716-1736, of the shogunate's reforms and of many surviving village registers.

Lower Yangzi.def: The rich rice-and-silk country of the lower Yangtze around Lake Tai and Suzhou - the Jiangnan of the record's Chinese sources.

MAFF.def: Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, whose design standards for fields, drains and reservoirs the record cites.

MLIT.def: Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, whose land-classification and river material the record cites.

Manning.def: The engineering formula for flow in an open channel from its slope, section and roughness; it yields a width only once four parameters are assumed.

Meiji.def: The era from 1868, when Japan modernized: its land consolidation, drainage works and row planting are the modern forms a pre-modern map must not show.

Meireki.def: The Japanese era of 1655 to 1658. Its fire of 1657 was the worst in Edo's history.

Mengxi Bitan.def: Shen Kuo's 11th-century Dream Pool Essays, a Song notebook of technical observation.

Ming dynasty.def: The Ming, 1368-1644, the dynasty of the great brick city walls.

Muromachi.def: The Muromachi period, 1336-1573, the age of the Ashikaga shoguns.

Nara period.def: The eighth-century period of the court at Nara, in which the jori land grid first appears in the record (743).

Nihonbashi.def: The bridge at the center of Edo where the five highways began and from which road distances were measured; the site of the shogunate's principal notice board.

Odoi.def: The earth rampart Hideyoshi threw around Kyoto in 1591, which fixed the city's outer boundary.

Pearl delta.def: The Pearl River delta of southern China: the low, water-cut country where the mulberry-dike fishpond was worked at its largest scale.

Phragmites.def: The common reed (yoshi): the tall grass of the reed swamp between open water and the sedge zone.

Polygonum thunbergii.def: Thunberg's smartweed: the trailing annual that follows the first weeds on an abandoned paddy, before the sedges take over.

Qimin Yaoshu.def: The sixth-century Chinese farming manual, the oldest complete agricultural treatise to survive, where the coop, the orchard and the rotations are first written down.

Qing dynasty.def: The Qing, 1644-1912, China's last dynasty, whose gazetteers and surveys supply many of the record's figures.

Qingming.def: The Chinese tomb-sweeping festival, at which families clear and tend their ancestors' graves.

Qingming Shanghe Tu.def: The Song handscroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival, the fullest surviving picture of a Chinese city's street life.

Roju.def: The shogunate's governing council of senior lords.

Rokugan.def: The empire these maps are drawn for: the Legend of the Five Rings world the campaign is set in.

Senbon Torii.def: The 'Thousand Torii': the tunnel of donated gates on the approach at Fushimi Inari, the densest form of the donation row.

Sengoku.def: The age of civil wars, roughly 1467-1600, before the castle towns: the age of the fortified rural warrior residence.

Shokuho period.def: The Oda-Toyotomi decades at the end of the sixteenth century, between the age of civil wars and the Tokugawa peace, when the first great castle towns were laid out.

Showa.def: The era from 1926; with Meiji, the modern period whose land consolidation produced the rectangular paddy grid a pre-modern map must not show.

Siku Quanshu.def: The Qing imperial collectanea of 1782, in which many older Chinese texts survive; the farming manual quoted here is read in its edition.

Six Chambers.def: The six clerical offices of a Chinese local government, housed at county scale as side halls flanking the yamen's courtyards rather than as separate buildings.

Song dynasty.def: The Song, 960-1279: when China's walled wards opened into shop-lined streets, and the dynasty the setting's demographics anchor to.

Spiraea.def: Meadowsweet: the low shrubs that come in on the drier margin of a reed grassland.

Spring and Autumn.def: The Chinese period before the Warring States, roughly the eighth to fifth centuries BC.

Sus.def: The pig genus; Sus bones in an excavation report are the bones of pigs, wild or domestic.

Tang dynasty.def: The Tang, 618-907: the dynasty of the walled, curfewed city ward, and of Chang'an, the capital Nara and Kyoto were modeled on.

Thousand Character Classic.def: The Chinese primer of a thousand different characters learned in a fixed order, and so used as a numbering sequence - here for a pauper cemetery's plots.

Tohoku.def: The cold, snowy northeast of Japan's main island: the country of the igune homestead grove, where the stable often stands under the dwelling's own roof.

Tokugawa.def: The shogunal house that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868; its era is the Edo period.

Toro.def: The excavated wet-rice village of the Yayoi period in Shizuoka, whose canal banks and paddy bunds were faced with the same driven sheet boards.

Wanli era.def: The Wanli reign of the Ming, 1573 to 1620.

Warring States.def: The Chinese age of warring kingdoms, the fifth to third centuries BC, before the empire.

Willow Palisade.def: The Qing dynasty's frontier earthwork in Manchuria, planted with willow along its bank - the one place a planting interval is written into law.

Yayoi period.def: The Japanese period more than two thousand years ago in which wet-rice farming and its first irrigation works appear, before the Kofun period.

Yuan dynasty.def: The Mongol dynasty that ruled China between the Song and the Ming, 1279 to 1368.

Zhengyi.def: The 'Orthodox Unity' school of Daoism, whose priests marry, live in households and pass ordination down the family.

aburaya.def: An oil presser's works: the wedge-and-beam press, the seed-roasting stove and the ox-driven mill that crush rape and sesame seed for oil.

abutment.def: The solid block of masonry or earth on the bank that a bridge's or a boom's end is anchored to.

akusui.def: The drain: the collector ditch at a field's foot that gathers the paddies' tail water and storm runoff, wider at its end than the supply that watered the same ground.

alluvial fan.def: The spread of gravel a stream lays down where it leaves the hills: a steep apex, a dry mid-fan where the water sinks into the gravel, and a spring line at its toe.

anaerobic.def: Without oxygen: water or mud in which the oxygen has been used up, where fish cannot feed and waste rots foul.

aqueduct.def: A built channel carrying water across country, sometimes on arches.

aquifer.def: The water-bearing layer of ground a well is sunk to reach.

artesian.def: Of a well: one whose water rises to the surface under its own pressure and runs without lifting, so its overflow has to go somewhere.

ashigaru.def: Foot soldiers, the lowest rank of samurai, housed together in row houses at a castle town's outer edge.

ashigaru-nagaya.def: The foot soldiers' row housing at a castle town's outer edge - the town's outermost ring of defense as well as its cheapest samurai housing.

assize.def: A court's periodic sitting to review cases; the Qing autumn assize decided each year which death sentences would be carried out.

asunaro.def: Hiba arborvitae, a cypress-family timber tree of the Hokuriku homestead grove; called ate on the Noto peninsula.

azemame.def: Bund beans: soybeans planted along the top of a paddy bund, a second crop from ground that would otherwise grow weeds.

azemichi.def: A walking bund: a paddy bund wide enough to carry a path, as against the ordinary dividing bund of one to two feet; the two to five feet the map allows it is a guess.

azenuri.def: The spring re-plastering of the paddy bunds with puddled mud, so that each basin holds its water.

azimuth.def: The compass bearing of the sun, in degrees clockwise from north; with its height it fixes where a shadow falls.

azolla.def: A floating water fern that lives with nitrogen-fixing algae on the flooded paddy and feeds nitrogen to the rice.

azuchi.def: The earth-and-sand butt at the far end of an archery range, into which the targets are set and the arrows stop.

backswamp.def: The low, poorly drained ground behind a river's natural levees, where floodwater stands and mud settles.

bailey.def: A walled enclosure of a Japanese castle - the innermost is the honmaru, the second the ninomaru, the third the sannomaru, with the moats between them.

bakufu.def: The shogun's government - the military administration that ruled Japan over the heads of the domain lords.

bakumatsu.def: The last decades of the Tokugawa period, from the 1850s to 1868.

banfang.def: The runners' shed at a Chinese yamen: an improvised lean-to against the inside of the compound wall, of no fixed position or size.

bansho.def: A guard office at a Japanese barrier station or gate, where papers and goods were inspected.

banyuechi.def: The half-moon pond dug in front of a south-Chinese house or village, its flat bank toward the houses - fengshui's water in front, and a store of water for fish, washing and fighting fire.

barbican.def: A walled outwork covering a gate. The European form's narrow neck keeps a mass of attackers from storming through, and by the same narrowness stops the defenders sallying out to meet them.

baren.def: The pad a woodblock printer rubs over the paper to lift the impression; its cover is woven from bamboo sheath.

basal area.def: The summed cross-section of a stand's trunks per hectare, measured at chest height - a forester's measure of how much wood a stand carries.

base flow.def: The steady flow a stream keeps between rains; where it holds the water level high enough, a channel can be fed without any weir.

batter.def: The slope of a bank's face, given as its horizontal spread against its height; a 1:1 batter is a face at forty-five degrees.

baulk.def: The unplowed strip of raised earth between two field plots, wide enough to walk on.

bed shear stress.def: The drag the flow exerts on a channel's bed, which is what scours it.

bedload.def: The sand and gravel a river rolls along its bed, as against the finer silt it carries suspended.

beishan mianshui.def: 'Back to the hill, facing the water': the fengshui seat that puts a house or a village with high ground behind it and open water in front.

beitang.def: The Chinese village pond system, the direct analogue of the tameike: millions of them watered about two-fifths of China's irrigated land into the 1950s.

berm.def: The bare strip of embankment top between a canal and the nearest plot, about a meter wide - room to stand for the yearly dredging.

board foot.def: A foot square and an inch thick: the unit sawn timber is counted in.

bodaiji.def: A family's own mortuary and patron temple, where its graves and memorial rites are kept.

bomori.def: The wife of a True Pure Land temple's resident priest, the 'guardian of the temple'.

boom.def: A floating barrier of chained or bolted timbers strung across or along a river to catch drifting logs, anchored to solid ground at both banks; a sheer boom is the hinged one that swings the logs to one side.

broadcast sowing.def: Scattering seed by hand over the whole field, as against setting plants in rows.

bu.def: A unit of land area the size of a tsubo, about 3.3 square meters; the cadastres give homestead lots in bu. Written after another unit, as in 57 tsubo 2 bu 5 rin, it means a tenth of that unit.

bugeijo.def: A domain's martial training ground, where its samurai drilled.

building fabric.def: The physical material a building is actually made of - old fabric being what still stands from its own time, as against a later reconstruction.

buke-chi.def: The samurai ground and the townsman ground of a castle town, assigned as separate districts by law.

buke-yashiki.def: A samurai residence compound in a castle town, enclosed by hedge or wall.

bund.def: The low earthen ridge between two paddy basins, a foot or two wide and about a foot high, re-plastered each spring so each basin holds its water; farmers walk the bunds to reach the plots.

bunsuiguchi.def: A division point: where a head race splits into the branch ditches that water each side of a field.

burakumin.def: The hereditary outcast community of Japanese history, who did the tanning, the executions and the other work the other castes would not; their quarter stood at the settlement's edge, by water.

bushi.def: A warrior of the samurai class; the word the sources use for the class as a whole.

byre.def: A cattle shed: the small building a farm keeps its draft ox or cow in.

cadastre.def: The land-survey register a domain kept of every holding, house and plot, from which lot sizes and holdings are tabulated.

canal corridor.def: The strip a canal takes between two parcels: the water with the bank margins along it, counted as neither pond nor dike.

cangue.def: A heavy wooden board locked around an offender's neck, worn in public for months with the crime written on it.

caravanserai.def: The walled courtyard inn of the overland trade routes, which watered and stabled a whole caravan from one courtyard well or cistern.

carr.def: A wet woodland of alder and willow on the drying edge of a marsh.

catchment.def: The ground that drains to a point, whose area sizes the drain carrying its water away.

catena.def: The sequence of soils and crops down a slope: paddy on the wet valley floor, dry crops on the well-drained ground above, woodland on the hill.

causeway.def: A raised road carried across wet or flooded ground.

center-pivot.def: The rotating sprinkler boom of modern American irrigated farming, which sweeps a circle of field.

chaoguan.def: The Ming and Qing customs barriers, which stood at commodity centers and on the Grand Canal and the strategic routes rather than at a county seat's gates.

chenghuangmiao.def: The City God temple that stood at every seat of Chinese local government, where the highest local official led the state sacrifices to the City God.

chi.def: The Chinese foot, ten cun. Its length changed over the centuries: about 23 to 24 centimeters from the Warring States period through the Han dynasty, and about 33 centimeters in later use.

chinju.def: A settlement's own tutelary shrine, the seat of the deity that guards it.

chinju no mori.def: The grove kept standing around a tutelary shrine - preserved rather than cleared.

cho.def: About one hectare (10 tan), the unit a holding or a village's fields were reckoned in; also a town block of that size. Land counted in cho is chobu (町歩): 5 chobu is 5 cho of land, about 5 hectares.

chonin.def: Townspeople: the merchants and artisans of a castle town's commoner wards.

chronosequence.def: A set of sites of different ages read as one sequence in time - fields abandoned five, fifteen and more years ago standing in for the history of one field.

chugen.def: Samurai household servants of commoner birth, hired by the season or the day.

coefficient of variation.def: A measure of how unequal a set of lengths is - their spread divided by their average - so a quarter means they typically differ from the average by about a quarter of it.

collector.def: The drain along a field's low line that gathers what runs out of the basins.

comb.def: The fan-shaped field layout these maps draw: a head race forking into a canal along each margin, with delivery ditches running down between the columns of paddy like a comb's teeth.

command area.def: The ground an irrigation system can reach by gravity from its intake - everything below the head race that the ditches can water.

confluence.def: The point where two watercourses join and run on as one.

coping.def: The small tiled roof capping an earthen wall, which keeps rain off its earth core.

coppice.def: A wood cut on a cycle - every 15 to 20 years the stems are cut to the stump and regrow - for firewood, poles and fodder; the floor stays open and the canopy young.

copse.def: A small stand of trees; here, the loose greenery of fruit trees and bamboo in the gaps between a village's houses.

corvee.def: Labor owed to a lord in place of tax - the work that built a town's moats, dikes and canals.

county seat.def: The walled town a county was governed from: the magistrate's yamen, and the market center of the countryside around it.

cribbing.def: A bank facing built of squared timbers stacked in an open box frame and filled with stone.

culm.def: A bamboo's stem: the hollow, jointed cane, a few inches across on a timber bamboo.

culvert.def: A covered drain carrying water beneath a road, a wall or an embankment.

cun.def: A Chinese inch, ten to a chi, so its length followed the chi's: about 2.3 to 2.4 centimeters from the Warring States period through the Han dynasty, and about 3.3 centimeters in later use.

curtain.def: The stretch of wall between two towers - the plain face an attacker meets, covered by the towers to either side.

cyanobacterium.def: Blue-green algae - the kind living inside the azolla fern that takes nitrogen out of the air.

dBA.def: A-weighted decibels - loudness measured the way a human ear weights it.

dS/m.def: Decisiemens per meter, the unit of water saltiness. Rice is the most salt-sensitive cereal, and its yield falls above about 0.9 dS/m in the field water.

daidokoro.def: The kitchen of a Japanese house, with its clay hearth.

daihachiguruma.def: The large two-wheeled hand cart of Edo Japan, pulled by men and confined by law to a few cities.

daikan.def: An intendant: the magistrate who administered a tract of the shogunate's own land from a local office.

daikansho.def: An intendant's office: the compound from which a tract of the shogunate's own land was administered - the model for the setting's county magistracy.

daikon.def: The long white radish, a staple of the household's winter vegetable bed.

daimyo.def: A domain lord: the hereditary ruler of a domain held from the shogunate, ranked by the assessed rice yield of their land.

daizu.def: The soybean - grown as a field crop of its own on the dry hem, and along the paddy bunds as azemame.

danna-dera.def: The temple a household is registered with and supports - the same relation as the bodaiji, named from the patron (danna).

daozuofang.def: The south row of a Chinese courtyard house, its windowless back forming the compound's street wall and its doors facing inward - the household servants' quarters.

degawari.def: The rotating fixed-term service on which a samurai household hired its live-in menservants (genan) and maidservants (gejo).

delivery ditch.def: The ditch running down from a supply canal between the plots, feeding each paddy through one intake and thinning as it sheds its water.

design cell.def: The size of leveled basin a field is laid out to, and the size every plot in that field is measured against.

desire path.def: A track worn by feet rather than laid out - the shortest or most easily walked line between two places; as few as fifteen passages make one.

detritus.def: The decaying matter that settles on a pond's bottom, colonized by bacteria - the third way a pond's manure becomes fish food.

dike-pond.def: The Pearl delta's farm loop: a pond dug in low ground, its spoil piled into a dike planted with mulberry; the leaves feed silkworms, the silkworm droppings feed the fish, the pond mud goes back onto the dike.

discharge.def: The volume of water a channel carries past a point each second - the flow whose square root sets the channel's width.

distributary.def: A channel that leaves a parent canal to carry part of its water onward, as against an intake taken off a river.

dituan.def: The Song corner tower, standing where a wall turns or at the angle of a barbican, made arc-shaped on purpose to reduce the face exposed to attack.

dobashi.def: An earthen bridge: logs laid side by side and covered with earth trodden level, so its deck is soil rather than plank.

dojo.def: A martial-arts training hall - a city institution; in the country, samurai trained in a yard or a cleared hall.

doma.def: The earth-floored working half of a farmhouse, where the hearth, the kitchen work and the animals were.

dooryard.def: The yard at a farmhouse's door - the household's own ground beside the house.

doshin.def: Low-ranking foot samurai and constables, serving under a magistrate's officers and housed with the foot soldiers at the town's edge.

dosojin.def: Roadside guardian-deity stones, set most often on the lonely stretches of a highway and near mountain passes, and usually at a village's edge where a road from outside meets its houses.

drainage ditch.def: A dug channel that takes water away from the paddies: the collector along the field's low line and its run onward to a watercourse.

drawdown.def: The letting-out of a field's standing water, when its drains carry their heaviest flow.

drill ground.def: The bare open ground inside a walled city where its garrison musters and trains.

dōba.def: The crushing floor of a Japanese ironworks, where the bloom from the tatara is broken up and sorted before refining.

ear mound.def: The monumental Kyoto mound heaped over war trophies, cited only as the upper bound on how large a heaped mound ran.

edauchi.def: Limb-pruning: cutting the side branches from a grove tree so it grows tall and clean-stemmed, as against topping it at a fixed height.

edge castle.def: A castle set at the settlement's edge, taking a river branch or a bay as the moat on its outer flanks, as against one at the town's center.

edge-runner mill.def: A mill whose heavy stone wheel is rolled on its edge around a circular track, crushing the seed under it; the oil presser's is turned by an ox.

eiro.def: The two Edo sentences that were actual imprisonment - life confinement and confinement in default - both imposed only exceptionally; the ordinary sentence was exile, flogging, a fine or death.

emergent.def: A tree whose crown stands clear above the general canopy; of a water plant, one rooted in the bed with its stems standing out of the water - reed, cattail, wild rice.

enceinte.def: The whole fortified area of a castle: every bailey plus its moats, of which the keep is about one percent.

eutrophication.def: The enrichment of still water with nutrients, which thickens its plant and algae growth; the shallow lowland dish ponds are the eutrophic ones.

exposure burial.def: Leaving the dead in the open at a set place rather than burying or burning them.

extension advice.def: The public advisory service that carries farming research to working farmers; an extension leaflet is present-day advice to today's growers, not a record of older practice.

extramural.def: Outside the walls - a suburb, a temple or a market quarter standing beyond a town's wall rather than within it.

fairway.def: The open water kept clear for boats to pass; a boom that spills into it obstructs navigation.

fall.def: The height a channel drops over its length - 92 meters over 43 kilometers for the Tamagawa aqueduct.

fascine.def: A bundle of brushwood or willow rods laid along a bank to armor it against the wash of the water.

fen.def: A Chinese land unit, a tenth of a mu: about 67 square meters.

feng shui.def: The Chinese practice of siting graves, houses and villages by the lie of hills, water and wind.

fengshui grove.def: The grove a village keeps on its windward, high side - the back grove of Chinese village planning - as its wall against the winter wind.

fertilizer boat.def: The barge that carried night soil out of a city to the farming villages, where a canal or river allowed it.

fetch.def: The open run a wind crosses before it meets a barrier; the longer and smoother the fetch, the harder the wind arrives.

filature.def: A silk-reeling factory: the machine works that took reeling out of the farm household.

fillet.def: The wedge of earth piled into the inside of an angle, which turns a sharp corner of a bund into a curve.

fingerling.def: A young fish part-grown, held in a nursery pond before it is stocked into the pond it will be fattened in.

fining.def: Converting pig iron to wrought iron by stirring it semi-molten under a charcoal blast so the carbon burns off - the Chinese chao, 'stir-frying'.

fish fry.def: Newly hatched fish, caught in the river and reared in small nursery ponds before they are stocked into the big ponds to grow out.

fishway.def: A stepped or sloping passage built beside a weir so that fish can get past it - one of the works that go with an intake.

flora.def: A systematic published account of the plants of a region.

forest litter.def: The fallen leaves on a wood's floor, raked up and carried to the fields as fertilizer rather than left to lie - which is what keeps a worked wood's floor light.

four gods.def: The East Asian siting formula that names a good site by four guardian beasts of the directions: flowing water on the left (the Azure Dragon), a long road on the right (the White Tiger), a pond in front (the Vermilion Bird) and hills behind (the Black Tortoise).

frass.def: Silkworm droppings, fed to the fish in the dike-pond loop.

freeboard.def: The height of bank kept above the water surface, so a full channel does not spill.

frontage.def: A row of shops or houses laid along a street with their fronts on the roadbed.

fudasashi.def: Rice brokers of the shogun's capital who warehoused the samurai's stipend rice, converted it to cash and lent against it.

fukada.def: A 'deep field': a paddy with deep, soft mud that mires to the knee, poorly drained until modern works.

fukugi.def: The evergreen tree Okinawan villages plant in strips around each house against typhoons and the winter monsoon.

funairi-bori.def: A boat-entry canal cut into a Japanese city so that barges float in to an internal dock - still water, never a live river.

gabion.def: A basket of woven bamboo or wicker packed with stones, used to build a weir or armor a bank.

gangi.def: A stepped landing notched into a faced riverbank, usable at any river level because the boat lies against a different tread.

gate market.def: The stalls and shops that stand outside a city gate, trading with the traffic that never enters the walls.

gate throat.def: The narrow passage through a gate structure, where traffic is checked.

gazetteer.def: A local history and geography compiled by a Chinese county or province - the record of what a district grew and built.

genkan.def: The entry of a house: the step up from the ground to the floored rooms, where shoes come off.

gentry.def: The landowning, degree-holding families of a Chinese district: the local elite from whom officials came and with whom a magistrate had to deal.

geomancy.def: Siting graves, houses and villages by the lie of hills, water and wind - feng shui and its Japanese kin.

geta.def: Japanese wooden clogs: a thong sandal on a wooden sole.

ginmisho.def: The examination room beside a magistracy's hearing court, where a suspect was questioned.

glacis.def: The open slope before a fortification that an attacker must cross exposed; the flooded paddies around a castle town served as one.

glulam.def: Glued laminated timber: a modern structural beam built up from bonded layers, stronger and longer-spanning than a sawn one.

glyph.def: The mark a map draws to stand for a feature - a shape chosen so the thing reads at map scale, which is not always the shape the thing has.

go.def: A tenth of a tsubo, about a third of a square meter - the fraction a surveyed site area is given to.

goemon-buro.def: The cauldron bath: an iron tub heated from below, the bath of self-sufficient farm villages.

gongxiefang.def: A Ming yamen's clerks' lodging: one named courtyard inside the yamen wall where the office's clerks were housed.

goten.def: A palace: the lord's residence and offices, standing inside the castle's baileys.

goulan.def: A Song performance hall: a railed or board-walled enclosure with a stage and seats, standing inside an entertainment precinct (a wazi), a large one holding audiences of several thousand. From the Ming on the word came to mean a brothel.

goyoba.def: The day office of a magistracy, where the routine paperwork of the post was done, as against the hall where cases were heard.

green manure.def: A crop grown to be plowed back into the ground rather than harvested, to feed the crop that follows it.

grow-out pond.def: The pond a fish is fattened to size in, as against the small nursery pond it is reared in first.

guanxiang.def: The suburb of streets outside a Chinese city gate, along the approach road, where commerce spilled beyond the walls.

gulou.def: A Chinese town's drum tower or bell tower (or the two combined), which sounded the gate-opening, the curfew and the night watches; the cheap form is a drum tower over the yamen's own gate.

gundai.def: A senior intendant governing a large tract of the shogunate's land.

hachure.def: Short lines drawn down a slope on an old map to show how steep it is, in place of contour lines.

haiden.def: The worship hall of a Shinto shrine, where people pray before the sanctuary.

half-river closure.def: A weir built across only part of a stream's width, leaving the rest of the channel open - the common old Japanese form, against a bar that closes the water bank to bank.

hanko.def: A domain school: the academy where a domain educated its samurai, one in nearly every domain by the end of the Edo period.

hansho.def: The small bronze alarm bell on a fire-watch tower, struck in a cadence that says how near the fire is.

hari-ma.def: The span between a building's beams - its depth, as against keta-yuki, the length along the ridge.

hata-ei.def: The Kanto rule under which the tax on dry fields was paid in coin rather than in grain.

hatago.def: A Japanese inn for travelers on a highway or in a town: at its humblest an ordinary household's shophouse whose back rooms took lodgers, at its grandest a purpose-built post-station inn of two stories.

hatake.def: Dry-field farmland - the unirrigated ground that grows grains, beans and vegetables, as against the flooded paddy.

hatamoto.def: A direct retainer of the shogun, ranking below a domain lord and above ordinary samurai.

hazakake.def: Rice-drying racks: poles in the field on which the cut sheaves hang for a week or two before threshing.

head race.def: The channel that carries water from the intake along the field's high edge to where it is divided into the ditches.

head works.def: The whole set of works where a canal takes its water from a stream - the weir, the intake mouth, the settling basin and the division works.

headman.def: The peasant head of a village and its district, answerable for its taxes and its order; his house is the largest on a village map.

headworks.def: The works at the head of a canal where it takes its water from a river: the weir that holds the level and the gated mouth beside it.

heimen.def: The setting's commoner caste - farmers, artisans and merchants - who in the Celestial Order are 'half-people', below the samurai.

hem.def: The band of dry ground above the paddy's supply canal where the dry crops grow.

hinin.def: The setting's outcast caste, 'non-people' in the Celestial Order, below even the commoners.

hinoki.def: Japanese cypress, a tall conifer planted for timber beside the cedar.

hinomi-yagura.def: A fire lookout tower: a town's tall timber watch tower with a bell, from which a fire brigade was called out.

hipposandal.def: A Roman iron hoof boot strapped to a horse's foot rather than nailed to it.

hirokoji.def: A broad avenue cut through Edo as a firebreak after the great fires.

hiyokechi.def: The fire-prevention open lots the shogunate cut into Edo after the fire of 1657.

hojo seibi.def: Japan's postwar consolidation of paddy into uniform machine-sized strips, on a 1963 standard of 30 by 100 meters.

hokora.def: A small roadside or household shrine, a knee-high shelter of stone or wood for a local spirit.

hongo.def: In Edo Japan the parent village (hongo) and the branch settlement founded from it (edago), whose tax registers stood in the parent's name.

honmaru.def: The innermost bailey of a Japanese castle, where the keep and the lord's palace stand.

houlongshan.def: The 'back dragon mountain': the wooded hill behind a Chinese village whose grove is kept as its fengshui forest.

houzhaofang.def: The rear service row of a Chinese courtyard house, behind the main hall.

hucheng he.def: The Chinese city moat: the ring of water dug around a walled seat, often made by turning a nearby stream through it.

hutong.def: A lane of old Beijing, formed by the blank outer walls of courtyard houses built side against side.

hyō.def: A straw bale: the unit rice, charcoal and salt were packed and counted in - of no fixed weight for charcoal.

ido.def: A well; where a farmhouse had its own, it stood in the rear corner of the earth-floored doma or in a back projection.

idobata.def: The wellside: the neighborhood's gathering point at a shared well.

idoyakata.def: The well house: posts set beside a well with a roof laid over them and nothing more.

igeta.def: The well curb: the square frame of timber or stone set around a well's mouth.

igune.def: The northern (Tohoku) word for a homestead grove - the belt of cedar, pine, cypress and zelkova on a farmhouse's north and west.

inkyo.def: Retirement: an elder who has handed the household to their heir, and the separate modest quarters they then live in.

intake.def: The opening on a stream's bank where an irrigation channel takes its water - the head of the channel, and the point where the dug ditch begins.

interceptor.def: The drain run nearly along the contour at the head of a field, catching the water coming off the slope above.

interlinear commentary.def: Notes written between the lines of an original text - in the Qimin Yaoshu, the treatise's own explanations of its own instructions, kept inside the quotation.

inverted siphon.def: A channel carried in a closed conduit UNDER a river or another watercourse, dropping and rising again by gravity instead of being bridged over it.

iriai.def: The customary common land of a Japanese village - woods, grass and scrub held by the village and governed by its own rules on who may cut, when, and how much.

iroha companies.def: Edo's townsman fire brigades, lettered by the syllables of the Japanese alphabet - forty-seven of them by 1720, about one to every twenty blocks.

iroha-gumi.def: Edo's town fire brigades, one per district, named after the syllabary.

irrigation ditch.def: A dug channel that brings water to the paddies: the head race, the supply canals along the margins and the delivery ditches between the plots.

ishigaki.def: The dry-stone revetment walls of a Japanese castle, run in straight segments with hard corners.

itabashi.def: A plank bridge: a deck of boards laid across its bearers, the small crossing a household lays over a farm ditch.

jetty.def: A landing stage projecting out into the water.

jiegao.def: A shadoof: a counterweighted lever that lifts a bucket from a well or a channel.

jiguchi-sen.def: The frontage tax attributed to Hideyoshi, assessed on the width of a house's street front - the popular explanation of the narrow machiya lot, which the Kyoto record disputes.

jin'ya.def: The seat of a small domain or of a shogunate intendant: an unfortified compound of residence, offices, retainers' houses and storehouses, in place of a castle.

jingtian.def: The 'well-field': the classical Chinese scheme of nine squares farmed by eight households around a ninth with the well - an ideal of the texts rather than a practice.

jinja.def: A Shinto shrine: the sanctuary of a local deity, with its gate, approach and hall.

jizo.def: A roadside stone figure of the bodhisattva who protects travelers and the spirits of dead children, standing at passes and in villages.

jokamachi.def: A castle town: the settlement laid out below a lord's castle, its samurai, townspeople and temples each zoned to their own wards by rank.

jori.def: The ancient Japanese land grid laid over the settled plains: one-cho squares, each cut into strips of one tan.

josui.def: An Edo-period aqueduct: an open earth cut from a river weir or spring to the city's edge, then buried wooden and stone pipes under the streets to cistern-wells the residents bucketed from.

josui-ido.def: A cistern-well on a buried aqueduct main: a shaft sunk mostly below grade that residents bucketed from exactly as from a groundwater well.

kabata.def: A spring-fed household water basin built beside the house, a regional form of Shiga.

kabu-ido.def: Village rules capping the number of wells, kept by the residents to limit quarrels over groundwater.

kagura.def: The Shinto ceremonial music and dance performed on shrine ground; the stage built for it is the model for a town's theater stage.

kainyo.def: The Tonami plain's own word for a homestead grove: the stand of cedar and other trees wrapped around each of its dispersed farmsteads.

kaji-ya.def: A smith's shop: the ordinary town smithy of one forge and a little yard, which also shoes horses and oxen where iron is worth it.

kakehi.def: An aqueduct: a wooden flume carrying an irrigation channel over a stream or a gully.

kamado.def: A masonry cooking stove; a brewery's rice-steaming hearth.

kame.def: A large glazed storage jar, the brewery's fermenting and storage vessel; heavy and cheap by weight, so made near where it is used.

kami-yashiki.def: A domain lord's upper mansion in Edo, the principal compound of their household there; a small lord's ran 2,500-7,000 tsubo.

kamiza.def: The upper seat of a hall - the honored end, from which a dojo or a reception room is laid out.

kan.def: A Japanese weight of 3.75 kg. Rice was baled by it; charcoal, which had no standard bale, had to be weighed at sale.

kanagashi.def: Loose-log driving: floating felled logs down the upper, unnavigable river one at a time, as against binding them into rafts on the lower reaches.

kanden.def: Dry paddy: rice ground that drains, so that when the water is let out it dries to an ordinary dry field and can carry a winter crop before the next flooding.

kannushi.def: A Shinto shrine priest, usually a hereditary office within one family.

karamete-mon.def: A castle's rear gate, typically opposite the front gate, from which the garrison sorties onto attackers held at the front.

karo.def: Literally "house elder": the senior retainer who ran a samurai household's affairs - in a domain lord's house, the senior councillors, who decided in council and lived nearest the castle.

kashi.def: A Japanese riverbank landing: a public quay, often specialized by cargo, with the warehouses, wholesalers and markets along the top of the bank. (The same romanization also names the evergreen kashi oaks; in a list of trees that is the sense.)

kaso-dera.def: A cremation temple: the temple whose precinct held the burning ground and ran the cremations for a quarter of a city.

kasoba.def: A cremation ground - in Edo a walled hearth inside a temple precinct.

kata.def: A fixed solo form of practice movements, drilled alone in a square of eight to ten feet.

kawara.def: Roof tile: fired clay tile, general on towns' roofs only at the end of the Edo period; commoners' houses were board- or thatch-roofed.

kawaramono.def: 'Riverbed people': the outcast tanners' own name for themselves, from the riverside ground their quarter stood on.

kawata.def: The Edo-period name for the outcast tanners' community, who held the rights to fallen animals over a territory and did the leather work.

kawaya.def: The privy: on a farm a single small building apart from the house, its pit the household's manure store.

kayabuki.def: Thatch roofing of reed or grass, the covering of nearly every farmhouse.

kegare.def: Death pollution: the ritual defilement of death and blood that Japanese practice kept out of the settlement - why executions, tanning and burial stand downwind, downstream and past the boundary stone.

keidai.def: A shrine's or temple's precinct: the ground of its approach, gate and halls - at a village shrine unfenced, marked by its arch and its wood.

keiko.def: Daily martial practice; a solo set-form (kata) needs a square of eight to ten feet.

ken.def: A Japanese unit of length of about 1.8 meters - the bay between two posts of a building, and the unit a lot's frontage was measured in.

kenchicho.def: The land-survey register: the book of every plot and homestead lot in a village, with its grade, area and holder.

kera.def: The raw bloom a tatara produces, crushed and sorted before refining.

keyaki.def: Zelkova, a tall broadleaf timber tree of the homestead grove's planting list.

kichin-yado.def: A cheap communal lodging in a town, the 'firewood-fee inn': a traveler slept on straw under a roof for a small fee toward the fire.

kido.def: A ward gate, shut at night to seal one block from the next: on a Japanese town street every tenement row and lane had its own, and a Tang Chinese city's walled wards had theirs, shut at the dusk drum.

kimon.def: The 'demon gate', the northeast: the inauspicious direction pollution was thought to leave by, where a city stacked its outcast quarter, execution ground and pleasure district.

kobito.def: The lowest grade of a samurai household's manservants, of commoner birth like the chugen and komono.

kochi seiri.def: Land consolidation: the Meiji-era program that regularized paddies into rectangles on true north-south lines, each on a road and a channel - the tidy grid a pre-modern map must not show.

koedame.def: The night-soil pit: a buried jar or plastered pit a meter or so across, in which night soil was rotted down for a few weeks before it went on the fields.

koji.def: The mold culture grown on steamed rice that starts sake, miso and soy fermentation; a brewery keeps a room for it.

koku.def: About 180 liters of rice: the unit of assessed yield, tax and stipend, taken by convention as a year's food for one adult.

kokubunji.def: A provincial temple of the Nara period, in a precinct about 218 m on a side.

kokudaka.def: A holding's assessed yield in koku of rice - the number every domain, village and stipend was measured by, whatever the land actually grew.

kokumori.def: The assessed yield per tan set for each grade of paddy at a survey - 1.5 koku upper, 1.3 middle, 1.1 lower - the figure a holding's kokudaka was built from.

komono.def: The lowest of a samurai household's live-in menservants, of commoner birth like the chugen, lodged inside the master's walled plot.

kon-ya.def: A dyer's shop: the indigo works, its sunken vats and boiling hearth inside a deep shopfront, its drying poles, racks and rooftop platforms filling the ground behind.

konara.def: A deciduous oak of the coppice wood, cut on a cycle for firewood and charcoal.

kondo.def: The main hall of a Japanese Buddhist temple, where its principal image stands; the largest building of a precinct, the biggest real ones about 150-190 ft long.

koraimon.def: A Japanese castle-town gate form, narrower than a Chinese city's gate tunnel.

kosatsuba.def: The notice board: a small roofed frame where the authorities posted the standing law, rate tables and ban lists, sited where everyone passes.

kumi.def: A group: a squad of foot soldiers, or a neighborhood association of households answerable together.

kumi-yashiki.def: Group residences: a block of plots where one squad of retainers lived together, on a castle town's fringe.

kumigashira.def: A village officer under the headman, in charge of a group of households.

kunugi.def: The sawtooth oak, a deciduous oak cut for firewood and charcoal beside konara in a coppice wood.

kura.def: A storehouse with thick plastered earthen walls, built to keep grain and goods through a fire that takes the wooden buildings around it.

kuramai.def: Stipend rice: the rice a domain paid its samurai out of the domain granary.

kurayashiki.def: A domain's warehouse-and-residence at the Osaka rice market, where its tax rice was auctioned to brokers.

kuromatsu.def: Japanese black pine, the windbreak pine of coasts and homestead groves.

kusaba.def: The service territory over which an outcast community held the right to fallen animals.

kyuhi.def: Stable manure: the stable's litter - straw and fallen leaves - mixed with the dung, trodden by the cattle and horses until it rots, and put on the fields.

landrace.def: A landrace is a local crop variety kept and selected by farmers themselves, taller and more varied than a modern bred cultivar.

lateral.def: A branch ditch running down-slope from the head race between the plots.

leat.def: A small engineered channel that feeds or drains a moat or a mill.

levee.def: The raised earthen bank that holds water in a paddy or out of a floodplain; a paddy levee is the bund, and is walked as a path.

lifang.def: The walled residential ward of a Tang Chinese city, its gates opened and closed by officials to the morning and evening drums; torn down under the Song.

lijin.def: Chinese customs barriers on the canals and trade routes - a Ming-Qing tariff post and a later Qing transit tax; neither stood at a county seat's gates.

lineage.def: A descent group sharing one ancestor - in south China the kin group that holds land in common, keeps an ancestral hall and gives its village its name.

lineage village.def: A village of one clan descended from a common ancestor - the settlement form of south China; the great ones hold forests of tens of hectares.

littoral.def: The shallow-water shore zone of a pond, between open water and the reed swamp.

liuchu.def: The six domestic animals of Chinese farming: horse, ox, sheep, chicken, dog and pig.

loess.def: The deep wind-blown silt of north China: fertile, free-draining dryland farmed without irrigation, so its crops live on the summer rain and on lifted groundwater.

lognormal.def: A right-skewed spread in which most values sit near the median and a long tail runs toward the large - the shape the cadastres show for house and yard sizes.

louzeyuan.def: The public pauper cemetery every Song prefecture and county was ordered to keep from 1104, on high, open, barren ground.

lulu.def: A windlass on a frame over a well, the usual water-lifting gear of north China.

machi.def: A commoner ward or block of a Japanese town.

machi-bikeshi.def: The chartered townsman fire companies of Tokugawa Edo, the 'iroha' companies.

machi-bugyosho.def: An urban magistracy: the walled office-and-residence compound from which a town magistrate governed.

machi-dojo.def: A private commercial training hall in a city, run for fees by low-ranking samurai and later by commoners.

machiya.def: A townhouse: a merchant's or artisan's house on a narrow street frontage and a deep lot, shop at the front and living quarters behind.

madake.def: Japanese timber bamboo, the tall bamboo of basketry, fans and flutes.

made ground.def: Land made by filling shallow water or marsh with earth.

magariya.def: The L-shaped farmhouse of northern Japan, with the stable under the same roof as the dwelling - a cold-country form.

mamian.def: The 'horse-face' bastion: a rectangular spur projecting from a Chinese city wall, spaced a bowshot apart so that neighbors cover each other's curtain with flanking fire.

maoqu.def: The last of China's five fixed canal grades: the small ditch that carries water into each individual plot.

masugata.def: A castle gate court: a square enclosure between two gates set at right angles, so that whoever comes through the first must turn under fire before the second. At the ends of a post town, the name for the place where the highway is bent twice at right angles to the same end.

matsu.def: Pine; the black pine (kuromatsu) is the windbreak pine of coasts and homestead groves.

meander.def: A loop a channel cuts in its own floodplain; how tight it turns scales with the channel's width.

meibutsu.def: A regional specialty sold as a souvenir of the place.

minka.def: A traditional Japanese farmhouse - a timber-framed dwelling under a steep thatched roof, its ridge on the long axis.

mire.def: A peat-forming wetland; the nutrient-rich lowland kind carries sedge, reed, cattail and alder.

mizugashira.def: Water-heads: the villagers elected to run the irrigation flow and its turns.

mizuguchi.def: A paddy's intake: the notch in the bund through which water enters the plot from the delivery ditch, one per plot.

module.def: The repeating bay a polder's ditch grid is laid out on: the distance from one lateral ditch to the next.

momi.def: Unhulled rice as it comes off the plant, before milling - the harvest that is spread on the yard to dry.

mon.def: The copper coin of Edo Japan, the smallest unit of cash; as the suffix of a building's name, a gate.

monk outlet.def: The older of a fish pond's two draining works: an upright boarded shaft against the dike, as against a sluice cut through it.

monzen.def: 'Before the gate': the neighborhood of shops and inns on the approach to a temple or shrine. In Edo, a gate town was a row of lay town houses built on land belonging to the temple's own precinct, facing its approach.

moso.def: Giant bamboo, the other timber bamboo of Japan, hardy to about -18 C.

mu.def: A Chinese land unit of about 667 square meters, roughly a fifteenth of a hectare.

muenzuka.def: The pauper's mound for the unclaimed dead, and the unclaimed dead themselves.

murataka.def: A village's assessed yield in koku, the number its tax was set from.

mushiro.def: A straw mat, about 90 by 180 centimeters - two to a tsubo - spread over the work yard to dry the harvest, and the unit the yard was measured in.

nagaya.def: A row house: one long building divided along its length into small tenements, each a room or two deep.

nagayamon.def: A gate cut through a long row building: a samurai residence's front range, with the gatekeeper's room, servants' quarters, stable and storeroom inside it.

nagewatashi.def: A weir thrown across a river to turn part of its flow into a canal's intake.

nakaboshi.def: The mid-season drain: in midsummer the paddy is emptied and dried until the surface cracks, then flooded again. Before modern times, as doyoboshi, it was done only in some places, where water was plentiful.

nando.def: A closed inner room of a Japanese house used for storage and sleeping; where a small household's servants slept, under the main roof.

natural levee.def: The slightly raised bank a river builds along its own channel from the coarse sediment it drops first - the first-settled dry ground of a floodplain.

natural village.def: The settlement as it stands on the ground - the cluster of houses - as against the administrative village the tax system recognized.

nawabari.def: The ground plan of a Japanese castle's baileys, laid out to the terrain.

naya.def: A farmstead's barn: the general work-and-storage building beside the house.

neige.def: The Grand Secretariat: the Chinese emperor's council of state, inside the palace precinct.

nengu.def: The land tax of Edo Japan, paid mainly in rice.

neribei.def: The Japanese earthen walls: plastered earth over a post core (neribei), earth on a stone plinth (dobei), and rammed earth up to a meter thick (tsuijibei); each carries its own small tiled roof.

night soil.def: Human waste collected from privies and composted as fertilizer.

ninomaru.def: The second bailey of a Japanese castle, outside the innermost one, often holding the lord's palace and offices.

noborigama.def: The climbing kiln: a long chambered kiln built up a slope, firebox at the bottom and chimney at the top, stoked in shifts for days.

nucleated.def: Of a settlement: gathered into one compact cluster of houses and plots, as against farmsteads dispersed each among its own fields.

numajiro.def: A 'marsh castle': a fort whose surrounding wetland was its main defense.

nunosarashi.def: Cloth-bleaching: rinsing dyed bolts in open running water, which is the dyer's reason for river or channel frontage.

nuriya.def: Plaster-faced construction: a wooden building rendered outside with earth as a fire precaution, one step short of a full storehouse.

oblique weir.def: A weir set at a slant, running diagonally upstream from the intake mouth instead of square across the stream, so it dams the shallow riffle and stands clear of the flood's fastest water.

ochiba.def: Fallen leaves: the forest litter raked off a coppice wood's floor and carried to the paddies as fertilizer.

offtake.def: The point where a smaller channel leaves its parent, at an acute angle pointing downstream.

ofuregaki.def: The shogunate's circulars, passed down to the villages, copied by the headman and posted on the notice board.

omamori.def: An amulet bestowed by a shrine or temple in return for an offering.

omoya.def: The main house of a farmstead - the dwelling itself, as against its wings and outbuildings.

onmyodo.def: The divination of direction and time by yin-yang and the five phases, by which a gate's auspicious aspect - a castle's front gate facing south - was chosen.

oshi.def: A pilgrimage agent attached to a great shrine, who recruited worshippers in the provinces, lodged them and guided them to it.

oshirasu.def: The white-gravel court where a case was heard, the litigants kneeling below the magistrate's raised floor.

ossuary.def: A place where the bones of the dead are kept together - here a low mound with one weathered stupa over the communal bones of the poor and the unclaimed.

ote-mon.def: A castle's front gate, at the head of the ceremonial approach; the rear gate (karamete-mon) is typically opposite it.

ote-suji.def: The ceremonial approach avenue from a castle town into the castle's front gate, with the offices of state flanking it.

outfall.def: Where a drain discharges what it has gathered.

outwork.def: A defensive work built outside the main wall - the barbican before a gate.

ox-frame.def: A timber frame set in the stream bed and loaded with stone: one of the materials a weir was built of before modern times, used alone or with gabions and brushwood and covered over with earth and gravel.

pannage.def: Turning pigs loose in woodland to feed themselves on fallen acorns and nuts, instead of penning and feeding them.

parapet.def: The low breastwork along the top of a wall or tower, which an archer shoots over.

perched river.def: Of a river: running above the plain on beds of its own silt, held in only by its dikes.

phytoplankton.def: The plant half of plankton: microscopic algae that multiply in fertilized water and are the first food a manured pond grows.

pig iron.def: The brittle high-carbon iron that runs from a furnace, useless for tools until it is refined.

plankton.def: The tiny drifting life of a pond, plant and animal both, which manured water grows in quantity and the fish eat.

plant association.def: A named plant community - the willow association of a river's sand and mud, the alder community of waterlogged ground.

planted collar.def: The planted band of dike ringing one fish pond - the ground between its water and the edge of its parcel, carrying the mulberry.

polder.def: Land reclaimed from marsh or lake behind an enclosing dike and drained by canals.

pollard.def: A tree cut back to the trunk every few years so that it throws a crop of straight shoots; dike willows were pollarded for withies.

postern.def: A small secondary gate in a fortification, away from the main gates, for messengers or a sortie.

puddling.def: Working the flooded paddy soil into a smooth, water-holding mud before transplanting - the peak of a paddy's water demand; a bund is puddled mud. In ironmaking the same word names a different thing: stirring molten pig iron under blast to work it into wrought iron.

qiandao.def: A towpath: the built way along a canal or river bank from which barges were hauled upstream. Shaoxing's dates to 815 and runs over 40 km, part of it laid on stone piers out in the water.

quay.def: A faced bank where boats tie up and unload.

rammed earth.def: Walling made by pounding damp earth in layers inside a timber form - the oldest form of Chinese city wall, and why those walls run straight.

rape.def: The yellow-flowered oilseed sown into drained rice stubble in autumn and cut in flower in March and April; its seed is pressed for lamp and cooking oil.

recharge.def: The water that soaks down to replenish groundwater - from a stream's bed, or from the paddies above it.

regime equation.def: The empirical rule for a stable unlined earth canal: its wetted perimeter goes as the square root of the discharge, with width, depth and velocity as smaller powers of it.

regulator.def: The gated structure at a canal's mouth that decides how much water passes into it.

renge.def: Chinese milk vetch: a legume grown in the drained paddy over winter and plowed under before the spring flooding as green manure.

return flow.def: The water that runs out of one district's paddies and is taken up again by the district below, instead of being wasted.

revetment.def: A bank faced with stone or timber to hold it against the water.

ri.def: A Japanese league of about 2.4 miles, thirty-six cho. The ancient ri of the imperial highway codes was far shorter, about 530 m, so thirty of them came to about 16 km (ten miles).

riffle.def: A shallow, quick stretch of a stream running over gravel - where an old slanting weir was thrown across, because the water there is shallow and out of the flood's fastest line.

ring dike.def: A dike thrown right round a village and its fields against flood.

riparian.def: Of the riverbank; riparian transport is carriage by river and canal rather than by road.

riprap.def: Loose stone tipped onto a bank's water face to take the wash of the waves.

river stage.def: The height of a river's water surface, which rises and falls through the year by many feet.

river terrace.def: A step of old floodplain left standing above a river as it cut down: dry ground above the paddy, and hard to water.

roji.def: A back lane between the tenement rows of a town block, closed by its own gate at night.

roson.def: The road village: a settlement whose houses stand in a line along a road, facing it from one side or both. Japanese geography sets it beside the linear village (ressen), whose line is a natural levee, a spring line or a waterway.

row house.def: One long building divided by party walls into separate dwellings - the nagaya form, a terrace in the English sense.

ryo.def: The gold coin of Edo Japan, the largest unit of its money, far above the copper mon.

ryobosei.def: The two-grave system: the body buried in a local patch, a separate venerated stone raised at the central temple.

sae no kami.def: The boundary deity whose stone stands at a village edge, a pass or a crossroads to keep evil and pollution from entering.

sakagura.def: A sake brewery: vat hall, koji room, steaming hearth, its own well and a rice storehouse behind a shopfront.

sally port.def: A small gate in a fortification through which defenders go out to attack a besieger and come back in.

salvage excavation.def: A dig made ahead of building work, to record a site before it is destroyed.

sand sluice.def: The gate beside an intake through which the sand that settles there is flushed back down the stream.

sando.def: A temple's or shrine's approach avenue, from the road to the hall, under its gates.

sankyoson.def: Dispersed settlement: the form in which each farmstead stands alone among its own fields, with no village street; the Tonami plain is the canonical case.

sanmai.def: A village's unsurveyed burial ground on waste land at its edge.

sannomaru.def: The third bailey of a Japanese castle, outermost of the three, holding the senior retainers' mansions and offices.

sanshaku-michi.def: The three-shaku farm path, about 90 cm: the standard width of a way between paddies, against the two-shaku (60 cm) farm water channel.

sara-ike.def: A 'dish pond': a shallow lowland reservoir ringed by embankments, as against the valley-head pond behind one dam.

sarae.def: The periodic dredging of a moat or canal: shoveling out the silt that settles in still or slow water.

satetsu.def: Iron sand, Japan's iron ore, smelted with charcoal in a fuel-hungry, low-yield process.

satoyama.def: The managed country between the village and the mountain: the coppice woods, grasslands, paddies and ponds a farming community worked and drew on.

schistosomiasis.def: The parasitic disease carried by standing fresh water, endemic where a village drank from its canals and ponds rather than from wells.

scour.def: The undercutting of a bank or a foundation by moving water - the reason a bridge's bearing sits back from the edge.

se.def: A Japanese unit of area: thirty tsubo, about 99 square meters, a tenth of a tan.

secondary forest.def: Wood grown back on cleared ground, as against the old stand a village kept.

seijoue.def: Row planting: setting rice seedlings in straight lines both ways with ropes or a frame - rare before the 1890s, so a pre-modern paddy is planted in a scatter.

sekisho.def: A barrier station on a highway, where travelers and their goods were inspected.

senmaida.def: 'A thousand paddies': the terraced-paddy site at Shiroyone on the Noto peninsula, 1,004 basins on about 4 hectares, the smallest half a meter square.

sento.def: A public bathhouse: an ordinary shophouse with a fuel yard behind it, one for every two thousand or so residents of Edo.

sericulture.def: Raising silkworms for silk: rearing them indoors on mulberry leaf, then reeling the cocoons.

settling basin.def: The basin at the head of a canal, immediately below the intake mouth, where the water slows and drops the sand it carried in before it runs on to the fields.

seven autumn grasses.def: The seven plants of the Japanese autumn, a conventional set of dry-grassland flowers - what a mown, burned pond embankment carries instead of reeds.

shahi.def: A reservoir's inclined intake on the pond face, drawing the stored water into the conduit (sokohi) through the bottom of the dam.

shaku.def: A Japanese foot of about 30 centimeters; ten to a jo, six to a ken.

shatian.def: The Pearl delta's outer, silt-built fields, as low and wet as the dike-pond zone but kept in rice.

shi.def: A Chinese measure of grain, roughly a hundred liters - the unit tribute rice was counted in.

shibai-goya.def: A playhouse shed: the boarded, temporary theater a touring troupe raised on shrine or temple ground, as against a city's licensed permanent theater.

shichiya.def: A pawnbroker: an ordinary shopfront whose bulky pledges fill two or three fireproof storehouses in a walled rear court.

shinden.def: New fields: land reclaimed and settled by allotment in the Edo period, each household given a homestead and a strip.

shirimito.def: A paddy's outlet: the overflow notch in the bund, set a little below the field surface, through which surplus water leaves the plot.

shironameshi.def: Japanese 'white tanning': hides soaked in the river for several days, the hair knifed off, the hide finished with salt and rapeseed oil alone - no lime, tannin, dung or urine.

shitsuden.def: Wet paddy: rice ground too poorly drained to dry out, which holds water even out of season. Harder to work, colder, and lower-yielding than a paddy that can be emptied, and it takes no winter crop.

shoin.def: The formal study with its alcove, shelves and window; and by extension the warrior household's formal residential style built around it.

shoji.def: The paper-covered sliding screen of a Japanese room; the summer set is woven of reed.

shoya.def: A village headman: the villager who answered to the domain for the village's taxes, registers and order. In a town the same title (nanushi) named a ward headman, who answered for their ward in the same way.

shubiki.def: The 'red line' on the map that marked Edo's official city limit.

shugenja.def: A mountain ascetic of the Shugendo orders; at Kumano these men were half-monk and half-layman, and sold talismans, amulets and souvenirs to the pilgrims they guided.

shuikou.def: The water mouth: the fengshui grove at a Chinese village's entrance, where its stream flows out of the village.

shukuba.def: A post town on a highway, with its transport office, inns and relay horses strung along one street.

siheyuan.def: The Chinese courtyard house: rooms on four sides of a walled court, its windowless back to the street; the servants in the south row.

sill.def: The bottom edge of an opening in a bund: an intake's sill sits just above the field surface, an outlet's a little below. The word also names the level bearing course an abutment presents to the beam that lands on it.

skimmer wall.def: A wall set across an intake's mouth that holds back the floating matter and lets the cleaner water below it pass.

sluice.def: A gated opening in a bank or dam that controls how much water passes.

sogamae.def: The total enclosure of a whole castle town by moat and earth mounds, as at Odawara and Osaka.

sokohi.def: The conduit through the bottom of a reservoir's dam, fed by the inclined intake (shahi) on the pond face.

solidity.def: How much of its own convex outline a shape fills: the measure of how deeply a parcel is bitten into, 1.0 being a shape with no notch at all.

sotobori.def: A castle's outer moat, ringing the town's inner wards rather than the castle itself.

species richness.def: The number of different species found on a plot.

spillway.def: The overflow that carries a flood past a dam instead of over its crest.

spring line.def: The belt at the toe of an alluvial fan where water that sank into the gravels re-emerges; settlements and paddies cluster there.

steading.def: A farmstead: a farmhouse with its yard and outbuildings.

stem density.def: The number of tree stems standing on a hectare of wood, of every size.

stilling pool.def: A basin below an intake that calms the incoming water before it enters the channel.

stone pitching.def: Stone laid by hand over a bank's face to armor it against the wash of waves.

strip footing.def: A shallow continuous pad laid near the surface under a wall or a bridge abutment, instead of a foundation sunk deep.

stupa.def: A stone memorial tower raised over relics or ashes - the marker over a communal grave, or the ancestral markers of a clan crypt.

subgrade.def: The prepared ground a channel or road is laid on, below its lining.

sugi.def: Japanese cedar: the tall, straight conifer planted for timber and shelter, and the mainstay of a homestead grove.

sugumagi.def: The Korean village-entrance grove that blocks the water mouth of a valley - the Korean analogue of the fengshui grove.

suid.def: A member of the pig family, wild or domestic.

suiden.def: Wet paddy, as against the dry field (hatake).

suimon.def: A sluice gate on a channel: a board riding in grooves between two posts, lifted by hand or by a windlass from a crossbeam above the water.

sward.def: Unbroken grass, mown or grazed, with nothing built on it.

tagoshi kangai.def: Plot-to-plot irrigation: water enters the head paddy of a string and cascades through the bunds from one plot to the next, so the interior plots have no ditch of their own.

taiping-gang.def: The great bronze or iron water vats kept standing full in a Chinese palace's courtyards and at its gates against fire.

takasebune.def: A Japanese river barge, roughly 50-60 ft long, poled and hauled on the shallow rivers.

take-yabu.def: A bamboo thicket: a clonal stand of bamboo, in most cases of nearly a single species, cut for its canes and shoots like a coppice.

tamajari.def: The gravel spread over a shrine's approach, laid to purify the ground it covers.

tameike.def: An irrigation reservoir - a pond made by damming a valley head with an earthen dike, sitting above the fields it waters, with a single outlet.

tan.def: A tenth of a cho, about 992 square meters: the strip a paddy was reckoned in. In a Chinese farm manual the same sound is another word, a manure pit dug in the ground.

tanada.def: Terraced paddies: flights of small bunded basins stepped down a hillside, each held by a retaining riser.

tangpu.def: The dike-and-canal grid of a Chinese polder district, its canals five to ten li apart.

tatami.def: A straw floor mat about 90 by 180 centimeters; a room's size is counted in them.

tatara.def: The traditional Japanese iron furnace: a clay hearth smelting iron sand with charcoal into a bloom of steel and pig iron over several days.

tatemachi.def: The principal street of a castle town: the one the front entrances of the townhouse and samurai plots range along, running from the castle's main gate.

tax-free plot.def: A field whose yield funds a village's own expenses rather than the tax assessment.

tedai.def: The commoner clerks of an intendant's office, hired from the local peasants and townsmen who knew the district.

tenshu.def: The keep: the tall tower at the heart of a Japanese castle - a fraction of the whole fortified area, which is mostly baileys and moats.

tensuioke.def: A rain-fed fire tub kept at a house's door and on its roof.

teramachi.def: A castle town's temple quarter, where the lord gathered the temples - often along the town's outer rim or at its road entrances, their spacious precincts useful in its defense.

tertiary source.def: A work that summarizes what other studies say - an encyclopedia, dictionary or reference entry - rather than presenting evidence of its own; the record takes a figure from one only where the entry's own references support it.

thatch field.def: Grassland mown for roofing thatch - one of the parts of the satoyama landscape a village worked, beside its coppice woods, paddies and ponds.

tillering.def: The stage after rooting when a rice plant throws up side shoots; shallow warm water encourages it.

toe.def: The low foot of a slope or a field, where the water collects.

toki no kane.def: The licensed time bell of an Edo town, rung for the hours by contract - a separate institution from the fire lookout.

ton'ya.def: A wholesaler-warehouseman of the Edo economy, who stored, sold on and shipped a trade's goods. At a post station the same word (toiya) named the head official who ran the relay office (toiyaba).

torii.def: A Shinto shrine gate: two posts and two lintels. Each is a donor's gift, so a well-patronized shrine has rows of them.

towpath.def: The path along one bank on which teams hauled boats upstream; it exists because of the boats and goes only where they go.

tozama.def: An "outside lord": a domain lord whose house submitted to the Tokugawa only after 1600, ranked apart from the hereditary vassal houses.

transect.def: A measured strip of ground in which a survey counts everything growing, so a whole wood is described from a sample.

tributary.def: A watercourse that flows into a larger one rather than to a sink of its own.

tsubo.def: The Japanese unit of area, a square about six feet on a side - the floor of two straw mats laid side by side, about 3.3 square meters (36 square feet). House floors and work yards were counted in it. In the ancient jori grid of fields the word named something else: one of the squares the grid was ruled into, one cho (about 109 meters) on a side.

tsuijibei.def: A rammed-earth wall pounded up in layers inside timber forms - a meter thick and three high on a castle - the heavier of the two Japanese earthen walls, against the frameless neribei.

tsuijimatsu.def: The black pines of an Izumo homestead grove, clipped flat-topped every few years - the one attested topping of grove trees.

tsuke-tsubo.def: A year's contract under which a farmer collected a household's night soil in exchange for rice or vegetables.

tsunaba.def: The 'rope place': a great rope stretched bank to bank to catch driven logs where a river leaves its gorge.

tudi miao.def: The earth-god's shrine: the small hall of a Chinese village's tutelary deity, kept at the village's entrance or inside a temple beneath the main altar.

tulou.def: The round or rectangular communal fortress-houses of the Hakka of south China, a clan under one roof.

ujiko.def: A shrine's parishioners: the households of its district, whose subscriptions paid for its gates and festivals.

umagutsu.def: Woven straw horse-sandals, worn in place of iron shoes and used up within a day's travel.

umaya.def: The stable of a farmhouse; in the L-shaped magariya form a wing under the house's own roof, warmed from the kitchen hearth.

umon.def: A walled-up postern: a small gate through a Japanese wall, kept blocked except when it is wanted.

understory.def: The shrubs and young trees growing below a wood's canopy.

ura-nagaya.def: A back-alley tenement row, its one entrance opening on the alley rather than the street.

usufruct.def: The right to use land and take its produce without owning it.

village district.def: The administrative unit a village heads and several hamlets belong to, named for its village.

wall circuit.def: The whole ring of a city's wall, measured round.

wanghuolou.def: A Song fire-lookout tower with its own standing brigade.

waraguro.def: A straw rick: the rice straw stacked round a pole after the harvest and drawn on through the winter.

wari-tetsu.def: The tatara's refined product: flat bars of forgeable iron split from the bloom.

water duty.def: The water a crop is owed per unit of land - for paddy about a liter a second per hectare, plus the one-off soaking that puddling takes.

water gate.def: A gate in a city wall opening onto a canal rather than a road, so that barges pass inside the walls.

water-mouth.def: The low point where a village's stream and track leave the valley, and the grove planted there to hold the water in - the shuikou of a Chinese village.

weir.def: A low dam across a channel that holds a set water level and sheds only the surplus over its crest.

weitian.def: A Chinese polder: low ground by a river, lake or the sea enclosed by a dike that holds the water out, drained and farmed - from the air a chessboard of fields.

well-sweep.def: A counterweighted pole pivoted on a post beside a well, swung down to dip the bucket and up to raise it.

wengcheng.def: A barbican: a small walled enclosure outside a Chinese city gate whose own gate is set off the line of the main one, so an attacker must turn under fire.

wetted perimeter.def: The length of a channel's cross-section that is in contact with the water; a canal's width follows the square root of its flow through it.

windlass.def: The drum and crank over a well, turned to raise the bucket.

withies.def: The pliant willow rods cut from a pollarded tree, used for baskets, hurdles and bank repair.

wokou.def: The pirate raiders of the 16th-century China coast, against whom the coastal counties threw up walls in haste.

wrought iron.def: The tough, workable low-carbon iron a forge can beat into tools - what refining makes out of brittle pig iron.

yagura.def: A tower or turret - on a castle wall, or a town's lookout for fires.

yaita.def: Sheet boards driven along a bank or a bund to hold its face.

yam.def: The Mongol empire's horse-relay post system, by which a rider changed mounts and rode on.

yamen.def: The walled office compound of a Chinese county or prefectural magistrate: court, offices and residence in a run of courtyards on one axis.

yashiki.def: A residence plot - a samurai's mansion lot in a town, or a farmer's homestead lot in a village.

yashikigami.def: The homestead deity: the household's own god, enshrined in a small hokora in a corner of the house plot.

yashikirin.def: A homestead grove: the belt of trees planted around a farmhouse plot as its own shelter from wind and sun.
