shelter belt.def: A band of trees and shrubs planted across the prevailing wind to shelter the houses or fields behind it; in this record, the farmstead or village windbreak grove.

terrace riser.def: The steep face of earth or stone that drops from one terraced field down to the next field below it; its slope face is kept cut like a bund.

shed people.def: Migrants of the Qing period, when the population was growing fast, who moved in great numbers into the mountain forests of central China and cleared and planted the slopes.

Omi.def: The old province around Lake Biwa, today's Shiga prefecture.

alluvial.def: Laid down by a river: alluvial ground is the silt and sand a river spreads over its floodplain, and alluvial woodland is the wet forest, in Japan alder and willow, that grows on it.

ukiyagara.def: A tall bulrush (Bolboschoenus) of shallow fresh water, growing with or beside wild rice (makomo) in a lowland marsh.

Tonami plain.def: A plain in Toyama Prefecture, on the Sea of Japan side of Honshu, known for farmsteads that stand apart among their paddies, each inside its own grove.

Honshu.def: Japan's largest island, the main island of the country.

shifting cultivation.def: Farming a patch cleared from woods or brush for a few seasons, then leaving it to grow back while another patch is cleared.

sanheyuan.def: The Chinese three-sided courtyard house: a main range with a wing projecting forward at each end, the fourth side a wall - the courtyard house with its front row left off.

chumon-zukuri.def: A farmhouse of northern Japan (Yamagata, Akita, Fukushima) whose front wing, projecting from the main house, holds the entrance and often the stable - an L-shaped plan like the magariya.

bunto house.def: A farmhouse built as two roofs side by side - the living rooms under one, the earth-floored work room under the other, eaves touching and a gutter between - used inside as one house.

waki-honjin.def: The second-rank lodging for lords at a Japanese post station: smaller than the honjin but furnished to its standard, raised audience room and all, and open to ordinary travelers whenever no lord was using it.

toiyaba.def: The office at a Japanese post station where the relay of porters and horses was run - sometimes part of the station headman's own house, one or two to a station, at its middle or at its ends.

tenma-cho.def: The quarter of a Japanese castle town that carried the lord's relay horses and the labor that went with them, placed as a rule close to the castle's main gate.

sukego.def: The villages around a Japanese post station that sent men and horses to the station when its own were not enough for the relay.

ekika.def: A relay station of Japan's ancient state highways, keeping a fixed number of post horses by the class of its road; the one excavated was a walled compound about 260 ft a side.

grass carp.def: A large pond fish that eats grass and plants; farmers swept cut grass and livestock dung into the pond to feed it, and its own dung fed the silver carp.

root-cut.def: Mulberry cut back to the root and grown as a small, low bush for its leaves rather than as a tree; the most densely planted form, about 8,000 to 10,000 a mu in the Pearl River delta and 800 to 1,000 to ten ares in Japan.

gabled roof.def: A roof of two slopes meeting at a ridge that runs the whole length of the house, leaving a triangular wall (the gable) at each end; kirizuma in Japanese.

hongawara.def: The heavy full tile roof of flat pan tiles and round cover tiles laid in alternate rows, the older and costlier of the two Japanese tile roofs.

karishiki.def: Green manure: grass and young shoots cut on the hills and the commons and put into the paddy before planting - the fertilizer that made a village keep grass ground more than ten times its fields.

magusaba.def: A fodder ground: grass ground where fodder, green manure and thatch were cut, most often the commons of one village or hamlet - also called kusakariba or kayaba.

kusayama.def: A grass mountain: a hill whose trees were felled and kept down so that it carried only the grass a village's paddies needed as fertilizer; a small one set aside for one paddy was a tazuke kusayama.

ichirizuka.def: A milestone mound: an earth mound about 30 ft square raised beside a main highway at every ri, in a pair either side of the road, each planted with a tree - most often an enoki.

keihan-cha.def: Bund tea: tea planted in a single row along the bank between fields, marking the boundary with the neighbor and breaking the wind.

pent roof.def: A lean-to roof of one slope set against a wall of a house, below its main roof.

Sagami.def: An old province of eastern Japan, roughly the present Kanagawa prefecture, southwest of Edo.

Kawachi.def: An old province of central Japan, the eastern part of the present Osaka prefecture, bordering Nara.

mid-trunk.def: Mulberry trained on a short trunk and cut back to it for its leaves, so it stands between a full tree and a root-cut bush; planted about 300 a mu in the late-Qing Yangtze delta, and 400 to 600 to ten ares in Japanese mid-cut fields.

fan palm.def: The Chinese fan palm, grown in the Pearl River delta for its broad leaves, which were made into fans and thatch; a fan-palm dike was a fishpond dike planted with it.

gable end.def: The triangular end wall under the peak of a gabled roof, as opposed to a long side under the eaves; a building "entered at its gable end" has its door in that wall.

Sanyodo.def: One of the great roads of ancient Japan's highway system, along which relay stations (ekika) were set in principle one every 16 km (about ten miles), each keeping 20 horses.

tsunoya.def: A Japanese farmhouse with a separate wing joined onto the main block, making an L; the name used in western Japan for the form called magariya or chumon-zukuri in the north.

sugoya.def: A Japanese farmhouse whose whole building stands under a single roof - the "straight house", as against the L-plan tsunoya or magariya.

rin.def: A hundredth of a unit, used in Japanese measures below the bu (a tenth); 57 tsubo 2 bu 5 rin is 57.25 tsubo.

Nakasendo.def: The inland highway of Edo-period Japan between Edo and Kyoto through the mountains, the other main route beside the coastal Tokaido; its post stations kept about half as many inns as the Tokaido's.

mitsuke.def: A mound or stretch of wall of stone or earth set at each end of a post town on the five great highways, marking where the town began.

through-passage plan.def: A townhouse plan with an earth-floored passage running from the street door to the back of the lot, the rooms beside it; the busy post towns built their inns this way.

pocket pond.def: A small pond among a hamlet's paddy plots - one of the small in-field features a hamlet's fields carry, with a rock or a grave island, and a town's do not.

toshiyori.def: An elder: at a post station, the deputy officers who helped the headman run the relay office (toiyaba); in a castle town, the town elder (machi-doshiyori), the leading townsman who ran the town's commoner affairs for the lord.

chōtsuke.def: At a post station's relay office, the clerk who logged every man and horse coming in and going out.

umasashi.def: At a post station's relay office, the dispatcher who assigned loads to the relay horses.

ninsokusashi.def: At a post station's relay office, the dispatcher who assigned loads to the porters.

kozashi.def: At a post station's relay office, one of the lesser staff listed after the dispatchers of horses and porters; the record does not say what a kozashi did.

aisle.def: A strip of floor added along one long side of a building, under the same roof carried further down, which widens the house a little without raising its ridge.

four-room type.def: The common farmhouse plan whose raised-floor part is divided into four rooms, beside the earth-floored doma; most larger plans are this one with rooms or a stable added.

Kaei.def: A Japanese era name covering 1848 to early 1855, which documents use to date a year; Kaei 7 is 1854.

hoonoki.def: The Japanese bigleaf magnolia (Magnolia obovata), a tall deciduous tree with very large leaves; one of the commonest trees in the homestead groves of Isawa in the north.

four trees.def: The four tree crops of the early-modern period - tea, mulberry, lacquer and paper mulberry - grown in fields for sale and processing. The shogunate restricted where they could be planted, and from the middle of the period they were grown as local specialties.

staggered shelves.def: Shelves set at offset heights in a recess beside the tokonoma, a fixture of the formal shoin-style reception room.

seed.def: The number a map is generated from: every choice the map rolls, such as which form a town's inn takes, follows from it, so the same seed always draws the same map, settling each choice a real place could have made either way.

Lingnan.def: The region south of the Nanling mountains in far southern China, roughly modern Guangdong and Guangxi, with the Pearl River delta at its heart.

Ikko sect.def: The True Pure Land Buddhist sect of Japan, whose temples in the age of civil wars were defended by moats and earth banks, with a self-governing town (a temple town) growing up inside the defenses.

guard city.def: A walled garrison town of Ming and Qing China, built to hold a standing military unit rather than to seat a civil government; a battalion city held a smaller unit than a guard city.

NACA.def: The “Network of Aquaculture Centres in Asia-Pacific”, which published, with the FAO, the integrated fish-farming manual this record cites.

black charcoal.def: Soft charcoal that catches fire easily, made by letting the kiln cool with the charcoal still inside before opening it; made in Japan from the late Muromachi into the Edo period.

fall line.def: The line straight down a slope, the way water would run off it; a thing laid along the fall line points directly uphill and downhill.

calendar calibration.def: The conversion of a laboratory dating of a sample, such as charcoal from a kiln, into a range of calendar years.

white charcoal.def: Hard, long-burning charcoal that is slow to catch fire, made by opening the kiln wide at the end of the burn to raise the heat, then drawing the charcoal out and smothering it under ash.

gōsha.def: The district-shrine rank in Japan's modern shrine registers: the chief shrine of a district of about twenty villages, one step above the village shrine.

sōchinju.def: A castle town's principal tutelary shrine, guarding the whole town rather than one quarter or village; Edo's was the Sannō shrine.

tateba.def: A rest stop on an Edo highway between two post towns, or at a pass: teahouses and stalls where travelers rested and horses or palanquins were sometimes changed, with no official lodging.

watashiba.def: A ferry landing: the place on a riverbank where the ferry boats set out and came in.

bojikui.def: A boundary post: a tall wooden post set up beside a highway where a post town or a village ended, lettered, it seems, with the boundary and the distances.

kanjo-nawa.def: A sacred rope strung across the road at a village's edge, most often at New Year, hung with charms of straw to keep sickness and evil out; commonest in and around the Kinki region.

michikiri.def: Cutting the road: the village custom of barring evil at the road into the village - a boundary god set there, a rope or straw serpent strung across the way, straw sandals offered.

ai-no-shuku.def: An in-between station: a rest stop between two post towns that grew into a street of shops, officially a village and in principle forbidden to lodge travelers.

gaison.def: Street village: a village packed tight along both sides of a road and living from it, with shops and lodging - the denser, trading form of the row village.

murakiri.def: The partition of villages at the start of the Edo period: each village made a unit of rule and tax with its own fields and a fixed boundary, drawn with an eye to its irrigation water and its rights in the common hills.

Chugoku.def: The western end of Honshu, between the Kinki region and Kyushu; with Kinki, the heart of western Japan's plow-cattle region in the 1886 count.

weilongwu.def: An enclosed Hakka house of south China: a central hall with wings, closed at the back by a ring of rooms for kitchens, stores, privies, pigsties and hen coops, built so its household could live self-sufficient inside its own walls. In front of it lie a rectangular drying floor (the heping) and a half-moon fengshui pond.

hsien.def: An older (Wade-Giles) spelling of xian, a county of imperial and Republican China, the administrative unit below a prefecture, governed from a county seat.

bansui.def: Rotation of irrigation water: which villages or fields may take water, how wide their channels may be and when their gates may open, fixed by rule, most strictly in a dry season.

bungi.def: A graduated stake set at the point where one ditch is split between two areas or villages, by whose marks the split is set.

treadle wheel.def: A small paddle wheel, about five feet across, that one person turned by treading its blades to lift ditch water about a yard up into a paddy; light enough to carry to wherever it was needed.

chain pump.def: The Chinese square-pallet pump (the dragon-bone wheel): an endless chain of boards drawn up a wooden trough, trodden by people or turned by an ox, lifting water a yard or two from a river or canal onto fields.

noria.def: A large water wheel set in a river, turned by the current, with tubes or buckets on its rim that lift water and tip it into a trough leading to the fields.

mizuya.def: A flood refuge on a farmstead: a storehouse, sometimes fit to live in, built on a stone-faced mound higher than the house, stocked with food and bedding for the days a flood lasted.

kawado.def: A shared washing place on a river or ditch bank: a footing or steps down to the water where vegetables and clothes were washed.

water pestle.def: A water mill that pounds grain: a stream turns a wheel whose axle lifts and drops a row of pestles into mortars, to polish rice or crush grain.

waju.def: A ring-diked community of the low river plains: villages and their fields enclosed by one continuous levee and bound together to defend it.

town ground.def: Land governed by the town magistrate as the townsmen's ground, where their houses and shops stand, as against the ground of daimyo mansions and of temples and shrines.

multiple city.def: A walled city made of more than one walled enclosure, as when a suburb outside the gate grew large enough to be walled in its turn.

Nipponica.def: The Japanese encyclopedia (Nihon Daihyakka Zensho) whose entries Kotobank carries, cited here by its entry on a word.

preceptor.def: A cleric of one of the setting's Orders; every town has one preceptor per Order, and a town preceptor serves in a town monastery, where the Order's monks live under them.

Sōtō.def: The larger of Japan's two main schools of Zen Buddhism; the temples of the Hiki register quoted here, the Aichi training temple with its meditation hall and monks' dormitory, and the Hirosaki lord's family temple are Sōtō.

Tendai.def: A school of Japanese Buddhism; several of the Hiki district temples quoted in the record, Anyōji among them, are Tendai.

Martial temple.def: In a Chinese walled city, the temple to the god of war, set opposite the Confucian temple across the main street, as at Pingyao.

kune.def: The Kanto name for a farmstead's windbreak grove, and also a hedge or a fence of woven bamboo along a plot's edge; the word itself means the line between two holdings.

kyogen.def: A short comic play of the Noh theater, performed between the Noh pieces.

heping.def: The drying floor of packed or plastered earth in front of a south-China house, where rice was threshed and dried; at a Hakka weilongwu it lies between the half-moon pond and the house.

Luban ruler.def: A Chinese builder's ruler marked in lucky and unlucky lengths, used to fix a house's dimensions; named for Lu Ban, the patron of carpenters.

Xiang-Gan.def: The building tradition of Hunan (Xiang) and Jiangxi (Gan) in south-central China, set beside the Cantonese (Guangfu) tradition.

Guangfu.def: Cantonese: the Cantonese-speaking inhabitants of Guangdong and their building tradition, whose villages usually keep their main lane at the front.

road magistrate.def: The shogunate's officer over the highways, who assigned their upkeep to the post towns and villages along them, and to villages off the road where traffic was heavy.

Imperial road.def: On these maps, a main highway of the Empire: the through road that links cities and post towns, as against a village lane or a field road. Where one runs through a city as its main street it is that city's Imperial spine.

Northern Wei.def: A dynasty that ruled north China in the fifth and sixth centuries; the farm manual Qimin yaoshu was written under it.

Heibonsha.def: A Japanese publisher of encyclopedias; "the Heibonsha article" is the entry from its encyclopedia, one of the reference works whose articles Kotobank reprints beside Nipponica.

jōgōe-chi.def: One of the ranks of a Sōtō temple, with the kata-hōdōe-chi and the zuiie-chi, at which the ninety-day training retreat was held in the Edo period and a full set of halls was required.

animal unit.def: A count of livestock in which beasts of different sizes are weighted to one common measure, so that a large beast like a water buffalo counts for more than a pig or a goat.

Chubu.def: The central region of Honshu, between Kanto and Kinki, running from the Pacific coast across the mountains to the Sea of Japan coast; Niigata is in it.

meshimori.def: A woman kept at a post town's inn, in name to serve travelers their meals (the name means "rice-server"), and in fact often an unlicensed prostitute, tolerated by the shogunate as an inn servant up to a set number per post town. Keeping such women marked a place as an inn for lodging, so a teahouse, which was only for resting, had to be built differently.

bakuhan.def: The Edo-period order of rule shared between the shogunate (bakufu) and the daimyo domains (han), which ruled land and people and fixed village boundaries.

boji.def: An older boundary marker: it marked the limits of a temple or shrine precinct or of a medieval estate. It was usually a post of wood or stone, sometimes a rock or standing tree. The bojikui on the Edo highways carried the practice on.

so village.def: A self-governing village community of the medieval period. As it grew, a village's boundary with its neighbors gradually became clear, before the Edo land surveys fixed it.

hip-and-gable roof.def: A Chinese roof that slopes on all four sides at its lower part and ends in a small upright gable at each end of the ridge; the roof of a major hall, ranked just below the full hip roof.

screen wall.def: A freestanding wall set facing a gate, so that no one can see straight through the gateway; the first thing on a Chinese temple's or yamen's axis.

ryobu.def: A small deciduous broadleaf tree, one of the trees of the young cut-over wood nearest a Japanese settlement, beside konara oak, hornbeam and alder.

shide.def: Japanese hornbeam, a deciduous broadleaf tree of the young cut-over wood nearest a settlement.

yamahannoki.def: The Japanese mountain alder, a deciduous broadleaf tree of the young cut-over wood nearest a settlement.

Imado ware.def: The unglazed and raku pottery fired at Imado and Hashiba on the Sumida, northeast of Asakusa in Edo: everyday wares, braziers, flowerpots, clay dolls and roof tiles.

Chinese-style gate.def: A Japanese gate type named for its Chinese-style roof (a curved, cusped gable), not a gate built in China. It marked a shrine or temple of some standing; Sano's district shrine Asahimori had one.

adept.def: In this setting, a monk of the rank that may marry and raise children. A married adept's family lives in an ordinary home near the temple.

initiate.def: In this setting, a lay person studying religion under a temple while working an ordinary job. A temple has about twice as many initiates as monks, and only a few of them sleep inside its walls.

Hui style.def: The traditional building style of Huizhou in south-east China, one of whose hallmarks is the horse-head wall: a gable wall rising well above the roof between one house and the next, to stop fire spreading.

Kyoto measure.def: The Kyoto standard for the ken, about 6.5 ft (1.97 m), larger than the Edo ken of about 6 ft; the frontages in this record are converted at the Kyoto size.

Shanxi merchants.def: The trading and banking houses of Shanxi province in northern China, among the wealthiest merchants of the Ming and Qing periods; Qixian was one of their home towns.

udatsu.def: A small roofed wall that some Edo-period machiya raised on the roof at the boundary with the next house, to stop a fire spreading from next door.

river office.def: The office at a ferry or ford landing (kawa kaisho, 川会所) through which the crossing was run; on the Tokaido it stood on one bank only, beside the notice board and the boatmen's huts.

eighty-eighth night.def: The eighty-eighth night counted from the first day of spring on the old calendar, about May 2 - a traditional date for starting the season's farm work.

Tiangong kaiwu.def: Song Yingxing's illustrated Ming dynasty encyclopedia of crafts and farming (1637), whose irrigation chapter gives the daily rates of the noria, the chain pump, the well-sweep and the windlass.

Nogu benriron.def: Okura Nagatsune's illustrated treatise on farm tools (1822), the source for when the treadle wheel was made in Osaka and how it spread.

Settsu.def: A city in Osaka Prefecture, named for the old province of Settsu around Osaka Bay.

county magistrate.def: The official who governs a county from its walled county town. Their jurisdiction covers the whole county, the town and its countryside alike, so the ground just outside the town gate is still under their rule.

tsumairi.def: A house built with its roof ridge at right angles to the street, so that the triangular end of the roof (the gable) faces the street. In Japanese towns it was the less common form: most machiya ran the ridge parallel to the street.

half-story.def: A low storage story over the street side of a machiya, under a low eave, rather than a full second floor. The domains held second stories down to this by ban, and in Kyoto it stayed usual except in large merchant houses.

ridge-divided nagaya.def: A nagaya split along its ridge as well as across it, so its units stand back to back and each opens only on its lane side; the cheapest kind of back tenement, commonly nine shaku by two ken a unit.

back tenement.def: In a Japanese city, the rented row houses (nagaya) on a narrow lane behind the street-front shops of a lot, with a well, a privy and a rubbish heap shared by the residents; the home of peddlers, craftsmen and day laborers.

Tensho.def: The Japanese era name for the years 1573 to 1592; "Tensho 20" is 1592, the year the filling of Edo's Hibiya inlet began.

tako-beya.def: A crowded bunkhouse where a labor boss lodged the laborers he found work for and kept them under his hand.

yamori.def: In an Edo town, the manager who lived on a landlord's tenement lot, collected the ground rent and house rent on the owner's behalf, kept the tenants' registration, passed on the town's ordinances, and was in practice the ruler of the back tenement.

Aizu.def: A district of inland southern Tohoku, around Lake Inawashiro; the towns of Inawashiro and Shiokawa lie in it.

Fuyu.def: A variety of sweet persimmon. The newspaper history this record cites traces it to a tree that stood, in the mid-Meiji period, in the bamboo grove behind a farmhouse in Kawasaki village, Gifu.

Diospyros kaki.def: The scientific (Latin) name of the Japanese persimmon, called kaki in Japanese: the tree this entry is about.

take-well.def: A household's own well in a piped town water system: filled by bamboo pipe from a parent well at the water source instead of being dug down to groundwater. Omihachiman's townspeople ran such a system themselves.

mokoshi.def: A skirt roof: a lower roof run round a building below its main roof, so that a one-story hall looks as if it had two.

Hoei.def: A Japanese era name, 1704-1711. A year given as "Hoei 5" is the fifth year of the era, 1708.

Taiseiden.def: The "Hall of Great Achievement": the main hall of a Confucian temple, where the image of Confucius is enshrined. At Yushima in Edo it is the hall of the shogunate's own school.

refectory.def: A temple's or monastery's dining hall, where the monks eat their meals together; one of the seven halls of a full Japanese temple, and a room of an ordinary Chinese one.

garan.def: A Buddhist temple's set of halls. A full one, the seven-hall garan, has seven buildings, and which seven differed by sect and era; the name was also used loosely of any great temple with many buildings.

dharma hall.def: In a Zen temple, the hall where the teaching is preached; one of the Zen sects' seven halls, standing where the older plan has its lecture hall.

contour canal.def: A canal dug along a contour line, so it stays nearly level across a slope instead of running down it; it can water only the ground below it.

mizunomi.def: A landless villager of Edo Japan: holding no assessed land, not counted a full villager and given no part in village government, living as a tenant, by labor or by a craft.

kadoya.def: A dependent farming household of Edo Japan, named for the gate-hut on its master's plot where it lived; the huts inside a larger farm's enclosure held such households.

kaisho.def: A village's meeting hall; in the Kinki region, around Kyoto and Osaka, it often stood inside the precinct of the village's tutelary shrine.

gōnō.def: A rich farmer-landlord of Edo Japan: one of the village landlords who grew from the middle of the eighteenth century, out of older landlord families or out of trade.

ancestral hall.def: A Chinese lineage's hall (citang) for its ancestors' rites, also where the lineage met and feasted; in a Cantonese village the halls stand at the front, facing the pond.

tsujido.def: A small open wayside hall on four corner posts under a tiled roof, with a board floor about two mats in size, built by a settlement beside a road for travelers to rest and later housing a jizo or other stone image.

koshin tower.def: A roadside stone of the koshin cult, one of the stones that stand together at the entrance to a village beside its dosojin.

Yoshimune.def: Tokugawa Yoshimune, the shogun of the Kyoho era, under whom Edo was first ordered, from 1722, to roof in tile and build in plastered, fire-resistant construction.

sutra house.def: The temple building that stores its scriptures, the sutras; in the Nara-period plan it stood facing the bell tower across the precinct.

melon-on-the-vine.def: A Chinese irrigation layout in which one long canal (the vine) links and fills many ponds and small reservoirs along its course (the melons), each storing water for the fields around it - a larger counterpart of Japan's parent-child ponds.

shoro.def: A temple's own bell tower, the building where its great bell hangs; one of the halls of the old full temple plan, and apart from a Chinese town's civic bell-and-drum tower.

nago.def: A dependent farmer of Japan tied to a powerful household, who rented from it the house plot and house as well as fields, and often lived on its plot.

yashikichi.def: A house plot: the ground a farmhouse and its outbuildings stood on, which a domain's land survey measured and allowed to each farmer, usually a few se.

curb.def: The low wall of stone or wood built round the mouth of a well, which keeps anyone or anything from falling in; seen from above, the ring that marks where the well is.

town grain.def: The scale a town or village map is drawn at, about 1 ft of ground to a pixel, fine enough that small features such as a notice board or a well can be drawn at their true size.

shugen.def: the mountain-ascetic order of Japan, mixing Buddhism with the worship of mountain gods; its practitioners are the shugenja

Kōshin.def: a folk cult that keeps watch through the night of the Kōshin day, which comes once in every sixty days; a Kōshin hall is its small place of worship

Yakushi.def: the Medicine Buddha, prayed to for healing; a Yakushi hall houses his image

Amida.def: The Buddha of Infinite Light, whose Pure Land the Jodo and Jodo Shinshu sects pray to be reborn in; halls to Amida stood in many villages before they became temples.

Shakyamuni.def: The historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, founder of Buddhism.

Fudo.def: A fierce guardian deity of esoteric Buddhism, shown holding a sword and a rope against a background of flames.

visiting grave.def: In the two-grave system, the grave a family visits and worships at, often in a temple's grounds, set apart from the sanmai where the body is buried.

myoden.def: A "named field": land recorded under the name of the holder who answered for its tax. A myoden landlord came from one of these old landholding families of a village.

sakutoku.def: The part of a harvest left after the lord's yearly tax. A sakutoku landlord let their land to tenants and lived on that share as rent.

hikan.def: A hereditary dependent of a powerful farming household, bound to serve it. Hikan held no house plot of their own and often lived in an outbuilding or a hut on their master's plot.

branch household.def: A new household split off from a family's main house and given its own house plot and land.

tsurube.def: The Japanese well bucket, and the gear that draws it: a bucket on a rope over a pulley, or on the end of a sweep's pole.

hanetsurube.def: The Japanese well sweep: a bamboo pole crossed over a post, the bucket hung at one end and a weight of stones tied to the butt, worked like a seesaw.

bargeboard.def: A board fixed along the sloping edge of a gabled roof, covering the ends of the roof timbers.

Owari.def: The province around present-day Nagoya, and the name of the senior Tokugawa branch house that held it.

kaigisho.def: A village meeting hall; a name used beside kaisho for the halls the Kinki region set up from early times.

nenbutsu.def: Chanting the Buddha's name; a nenbutsu hall was a hall for that chanting, and in older times one of the places a village meeting was held.

festival lodging.def: The house that hosted a village festival; some villages held their meeting there after the festival.

purlin.def: A roof beam running along the length of a building under the rafters; a Chinese hall's depth is counted in purlins - the rear halls at Langtou, of thirteen purlins, are 8.5 to 9 meters deep.

three-bay two-corridor house.def: The common house of a Cantonese village, three bays wide, built in rows behind the village's ancestral halls.

honbyakusho.def: The landholding farmers of an Edo-period village, who made up most of the village meeting.

komae.def: The small farmers of an Edo-period village, below the officials and leading men; later in the period they came to take part in the village meeting.

hirakata.def: The ordinary villagers of an Edo-period village, below the officials and leading men; named with the komae as those who later joined the village meeting.

Daimyōjin.def: A title of honor given to a Shinto god, "great bright deity", as in Hikawa Daimyōjin, the god of a Hikawa shrine. It is not the title of a lord (daimyo).

monto.def: The followers of Jodo Shinshu, the Shin sect; the Aki monto were its followers in Aki, the old province around Hiroshima, where cremation was the custom.

kō.def: A lay devotional society of a settlement's households, such as a pilgrimage confraternity that sent its members to a distant temple or shrine, which could own a shared facility such as a cremation ground its members built themselves.

two-grave.def: A custom in which the dead are buried at one grave, the burial grave, set apart from the houses, while a second grave nearer home or at the temple, the visiting grave, is the one the family visits.

fire bed.def: The spot at a cremation ground where the pyre of wood or straw was laid and the body burned.

Keio.def: The Japanese era name for the years 1865 to 1868, the last years of the shogunate; "Keio 3" is 1867.

swept collar.def: A strip of bare, swept ground kept around a shrine hall, an arch or a grave plot, clear of the scrub around it. It is recorded only in modern custom with no date, so the maps draw none.

Tanabata.def: The festival of the seventh day of the seventh month. In many regions that day was also counted the first day of Bon (nanuka-bon), when graves and the paths to them were cleaned to prepare for welcoming the spirits.

firebox.def: The combustion chamber at the foot of a climbing kiln, where the wood fire is fed; the firing chambers climb the slope above it and the chimney stands at the top.

stoke mouth.def: The opening at the foot of a kiln through which the fire is fed with wood during a firing.

Mino.def: An old province of central Japan, in present-day southern Gifu, and one of its great pottery districts; the Motoyashiki kiln stands there.

kiln house.def: A pottery business - the household and workshop that made and fired wares (窯元, kamamoto); in the porcelain villages several of them shared one great climbing kiln.

koaza.def: A small named section of land within an ō-aza, the district of a village; the smallest named division of a village's ground.

Kansai.def: The region of west-central Honshu around Kyoto, Osaka and Nara, the old capital region; the Kinai lies at its heart.

Ou.def: The old name for the northeast of Honshu, the two provinces of Mutsu and Dewa, which Yanagita counts among the regions where household graves were many.

country monk.def: In this setting, the one tax-free religious figure of a village district, who tends the village's shrine; their dwelling may double as the shrine itself.

Meiwa.def: The Japanese era name for the years 1764 to 1772; a date written "Meiwa 2" is 1765.

Nehan gate.def: A gate of a temple or mausoleum named for nehan, the Japanese word for nirvana: the Buddha's final release from rebirth.

levy storehouse.def: A storehouse in an intendant's office for what was paid in as levies other than the rice tax - the unjo charged on trades, fisheries and the like.

Echigo.def: An old province on the Sea of Japan coast of Honshu, the modern Niigata prefecture.

sub-temple.def: A small temple inside a great temple's precinct and belonging to it, with its own walled lot and its own monks. Zojoji held forty-eight of them and Kan'ei-ji thirty-six.

unconfined groundwater.def: Groundwater with no watertight layer sealed above it, so its top is the open water table itself - where that table lies shallow, a plain dug well reaches it.

cloister.def: A roofed corridor running round a temple's central court. It closes the court on its sides and joins the gate to the main hall.

hall of the Heavenly Kings.def: In a Chinese temple, the gate hall on the axis that holds images of the four guardian kings of the Buddhist world. At Quanzhou's Kaiyuan temple it is also the main gate.

ordination platform.def: A raised stone terrace in a temple where monks take their vows. The Kaiyuan temple of Quanzhou sets one on its axis behind the main hall.

gate-land.def: Ground in front of a temple or shrine gate, laid out as narrow, deep house lots, so that town houses line the street and the temple stands behind them at the end of an approach (see monzen).

field grain.def: The direction a village's paddy plots and their bunds run; it may follow the compass or the fall line, or drift off both with the region or the ground.

valley pond.def: A reservoir pond dammed in a valley above the plain, whose water is released down into the dish ponds on the flat and from them to the fields.

kaison.def: A lump village: a Japanese settlement whose houses are gathered irregularly in a lump, typically at a hill's foot, on a river terrace, or at a highway crossing where water can be got.

retsuson.def: A line village: a Japanese village whose houses stand in a line along a natural levee or a spring line at a hill's foot.

Rinzai.def: One of Japan's two main Zen Buddhist sects, beside Soto.

Nichiren.def: A Japanese Buddhist sect founded in the 13th century by the monk Nichiren, centered on the Lotus Sutra.

Hokke.def: The "Lotus" sect: a name for the Nichiren line of Japanese Buddhism and for some of the schools that split from it; Kanazawa's plan counts its Nichiren and Hokke temples separately.

horita.def: A raised paddy of the Japanese waju: part of a poorly drained paddy dug out and the mud piled on the rest, so the rice stands on long ridges just above the water and the dug strips between are channels for a field boat.

hakehi.def: A drain culvert through a waju's ring dike, shut while the river outside stood higher than the fields and opened when it fell, so the polder's standing water ran out by gravity.

warichi.def: The Edo-period custom of re-dividing a village's fields among its landholders by lot every so many years, so that good and bad ground, and the risk of flood, were shared out evenly.

Taiji.def: In Chinese thought, the one whole that divides into yin and yang - which is why the Hakka read a half-moon pond (yin) and the mound behind the house (yang) as the two halves of one arrangement.

metamorphosis fengshui.def: The Taiwan Hakka Museum's English name for the school of fengshui its page on half-moon ponds describes: a house built lower at the front and higher at the back, so that a household's luck rises step by step, with the half-moon pond and the mound behind the house read as yin and yang.

tezuki.def: A junior official of a shogunate intendant's office, ranked with the tedai; the tezuki and tedai lived in the huts and rowhouses on the office grounds.

rolled.def: Laid out by the map program from a random starting value rather than placed by hand; a rolled village is one whose houses the program seated.

kokuga.def: The provincial government office of Japan's ancient imperial state: the governor's halls around a south-facing court, in a walled district of their own in the provincial town.

Tenmangu.def: A shrine to Tenjin, the deified courtier-scholar Sugawara no Michizane, patron of learning; "Tenjin shrine" and "Tenmangu" name the same kind of shrine.

offering hall.def: At a Shinto shrine, the hall between the worship hall and the sanctuary where offerings to the kami are presented; often joined to both under one roof.

tachimuba.def: A station that the shogunate's intendants set up at a port of call on the tax-rice shipping route. Castle-rice ships were protected there and their loads were strictly inspected.

castle rice.def: The shogunate's own tax rice (御城米), shipped to Edo on hired vessels under official protection and inspection.

adze.def: A woodworker's cutting tool with its blade set crosswise to the handle, swung to shape and smooth the faces of timbers. On a storehouse frame, the marks it leaves date and grade the work.

se-machi.def: An old land-register way of counting the paddies in a terraced plot: "one tan, four se-machi" records one tan of terrace made up of four separate paddies.

fault scarp.def: A steep face of ground left where the earth has shifted along a fault; at Sakaori, the steep west side of the valley, where the walls are highest.

kokuso.def: The hereditary chief priest of the Izumo shrine in Japan, an office passed from father to son for more than eighty generations.

daoshi.def: A Daoist priest; the married ones who lived at home rather than in a temple were called huoju or sanju daoshi.

mushiko.def: A window of close-set, plaster-covered vertical slats in the low upper floor of a Kyoto town house.

kokera.def: A roof of thin wooden shingles laid in overlapping courses; the Takayama jin'ya's office used it for part of its roof.

odoko.def: A great display alcove: the broad ceremonial alcove of a formal reception room, whose width marked the rank of the house - at Takayama Jin'ya's entrance room it is 2.5 ken wide, the mark of a 100,000-koku rank.

noshi-buki.def: A roof laid with wooden boards: with kokera shingle, one of the plank roofings that cover the buildings of Takayama Jin'ya, where snow wore out the tiles of the day and timber was easy to get.

governor-general.def: In Qing China, the highest provincial official, over one province or several; their yamen stood in a provincial seat, as the Zhili governor-general's did at Baoding.

kokucho.def: The central government office inside an ancient Japanese kokuga (provincial office district), whose main hall was the seat of provincial rule.

admonition arch.def: An arch on a Qing yamen's central axis, between the ceremonial gate and the great hall; at the Zhili governor-general's yamen it was the third thing a visitor passed through after the main gate.

water teahouse.def: In the Edo period, a teahouse where a passer-by sat to rest over tea, as twenty did in a row on Sensoji's approach; a rest stop rather than an eating house.

open-ended dike.def: A river dike built in separate lengths with gaps left between them, so that a flood spreads through the gaps over the low ground behind and loses its force - with the waju's ring dike, one of the old Japanese ways of building dikes before continuous ones.

jito.def: In medieval Japan, a steward the warrior government set over a piece of land; in the Edo period, the name for a retainer who held villages as a fief, and who was still bound to live in the castle town.

gokenin.def: A direct retainer of the Tokugawa shogunate ranking below a bannerman (hatamoto), holding a smaller stipend and without the right of audience with the shogun.

katemeshi.def: Rice cooked together with coarse grain such as barley or millet, and with tubers, radish or greens, to make it go further - the everyday meal of Edo-period farm villages, even in paddy districts.

Censorate.def: In Ming and Qing China, the capital's office of censors, who watched over officials and reported their misconduct; at Beijing it stood west of the Daqing gate among the judicial offices.

Daqing gate.def: The gate at the head of the palace approach in Qing Beijing; the ministries and courts of the capital were ranged in compounds on either side of it.

memorial arch.def: A freestanding ceremonial gateway, in China a yamen's outside the gate by the street, that marks the office to passersby.

ceremonial gate.def: The second gate on a Chinese yamen's north-south axis, behind the main gate and before the courts of the offices.

admonition pavilion.def: A small pavilion on a Chinese yamen's central axis, behind the ceremonial gate, standing where other yamens raised an admonition arch.

dobu.def: A small open ditch carrying rain and waste water - before a house front, or under the boards down the middle of a back alley - narrow enough to step over.

field boat.def: A small, flat-bottomed boat for moving through waterlogged paddies and along the channels dug between horita strips, carrying people, seedlings and harvest.

overlay.def: A cash crop drawn over part of a village's rice field on the ground that suits it - a fishpond with mulberry on its dikes or a lotus bed on the lowest, wettest plots, or a tea garden on the lower hillside.

Dunhuang.def: An oasis town in northwest China on the old overland trade road. Its Buddhist cave library kept medieval monastery papers, among them registers of what a monastery took in and paid out.

Mogao caves.def: The Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff at Dunhuang, paid for by patrons over many centuries.

gold paper.def: Paper, often marked with gold, that believers give to a Chinese temple to be burned as an offering.

Shen Kuo.def: A Song dynasty scholar-official who wrote the record of the Wanchun polder, whose restoration was taken up in 1061, that the research quotes on how the polder's dike was built and planted.

Dacheng Hall.def: The main hall of a Confucian temple (a wenmiao), where Confucius's tablet or image is enshrined and the state sacrifices to him are offered; the name means "Hall of Great Perfection."

dobuita.def: The ditch boards laid end to end down the middle of a back alley, covering its dobu and making the path people walk on.

kaishochi.def: The open lot left in the middle of each 60-ken (about 120 m) square block of Edo's commoner land, behind the town lots that lined the streets.

kaibori.def: Draining a pond out of season to dredge the silt from its bottom and catch its fish; the dredged mud went onto the fields as fertilizer.

Kan'ei.def: A Japanese era name, 1624 to 1644, early in the Edo period.

bondservant.def: In medieval Japan, an unfree servant (genin) bound to a warrior household, who lived in its row houses and worked the paddy and fields before its gate.

Northern and Southern Courts.def: The period from 1336 to 1392, when two rival imperial courts, one at Kyoto and one at Yoshino, each claimed the throne and warriors fought for one or the other.

Zhouli.def: The Rites of Zhou, a classical Chinese text setting out the offices and rules of the Zhou state; it required trees planted beside the roads of the suburbs and the countryside.

Zhou dynasty.def: The ancient Chinese dynasty under which, by its classical texts, trees were planted along both sides of official roads; the Northern Zhou was a later, short-lived northern state of the 6th century.

Western Wei.def: A short-lived Chinese state of the mid-6th century in the north-west, under which distance was marked by an earth mound at every li beside the road, later replaced by pagoda trees.

pagoda tree.def: The Chinese scholar tree (huai, 槐), a broad shade tree planted along Chinese official roads - under the Western Wei in place of the earth distance mounds, and by a Yuan edict beside elm and willow.

storehouse-built.def: Of a townhouse: built the way a storehouse (kura) is built, with thick earth-plastered walls against fire, and standing on the street front. It was Edo's way, the opposite of Kyoto's, where the storehouse stood at the back of the lot.

kamidana.def: A small shelf-shrine to the gods, set high on a wall. The traditional Edo-period practice hall did not have one; a Ministry of Education meeting of 1936 made one required in school halls, under State Shinto.

iai.def: The Japanese art of drawing the sword and cutting in one movement. At a large domain school it was taught in its own practice hall, apart from fencing and the spear.

jujutsu.def: The Japanese art of fighting unarmed or lightly armed, by throws, holds and strikes. From the mid-Edo period its practice centered on free sparring (randori), and it came indoors onto board or tatami floors.

State Shinto.def: The Japanese state's organization of Shinto as a national observance from the Meiji era until 1945. Under it, the shrine shelf became a required fitting of school practice halls in 1936.

naginata.def: A Japanese pole weapon with a long curved blade, rendered "halberd" in English. At a large domain school it was taught in the same hall as iai and jujutsu.

throat.def: The mouth of a branch channel where it leaves or joins a larger one - its first short stretch, whose heading decides whether the junction is swept with the current.

contour.def: A line across the ground at one elevation. A drain laid along the contour runs level across the slope, so the water from the fields above falls into it along its whole length.

kang.def: A long raised platform of brick or earth, heated from beneath by a flue, that served as the bed in a north-Chinese house or inn; one in a carters' inn slept twenty and more.

mise.def: The board-floored shop room at the street front of a townhouse, where goods were sold or trade was done; in an inn built on the townhouse plan it stood beside the earth-floored passage.

sensei.def: A teacher of a martial art - here the master who heads a dojo, lives by its teaching and takes enrolled students.

ritsuryo.def: The ancient Japanese state's codes of law and government, modeled on China's; under them the capitals were run ward by ward, with a head over each ward who checked its households and pressed its labor levies.

time bell.def: A bell rung at set hours to tell a city the time; in Edo its upkeep was one of the running costs the wards paid.

fire brigade's standard.def: The emblem on a pole that a town's fire brigade carried as its sign (Japanese *matoi*); in Edo the wards shared its cost.

bo.def: A ward of an ancient Japanese capital's grid, bounded by the main streets and cut by lanes into blocks (machi); 90 jo on a side at Fujiwara-kyo and 180 jo at Heijo-kyo.

Fujiwara-kyo.def: The earliest of Japan's gridded capitals, before Heijo-kyo and Heian-kyo, whose wards were 90 jo on a side, each cut into four blocks.

jobo.def: The grid plan of the ancient Japanese capitals: east-west rows (jo) and north-south columns of wards (bo), each ward cut by lanes into blocks (machi).

Taiho code.def: An early Japanese law code from which the plan of the capital Fujiwara-kyo is inferred.

shigyo-hachimon.def: The Heian capital's rule for dividing a block (machi) into 32 house lots, four across by eight down, each 5 jo by 10 jo, facing the north-south streets.

eel's bed.def: A town lot with a narrow frontage on the street and a long depth behind it, like the Kyoto town-house lots about 3 ken wide; the phrase translates the Japanese name for such a plot.

dorui.def: A Japanese earth bank raised as a rampart, usually from the spoil of the ditch dug beside it, about 2 to 3 m high, with a fence or wall along its flat top.

yaguramon.def: A Japanese castle gate with a guard tower built over its passage; in a masugata it is the inner of the two gates.

xunjiansi.def: A Chinese patrol and inspection post below the county, under a minor officer, set against bandits and pirates and answering to the local magistrate.

wet-tint haze.def: The hazy blue tint the map lays over wet ground to mark it as marsh or waterlogged.

JSIDRE.def: The Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering, whose journal publishes research on farm water, reservoirs and rural land.

back marsh.def: The low, poorly drained ground behind a river's natural levees, often holding ponds and old ox-bow lakes; in Japan it was traditionally cleared and used as paddy.

spur.def: A tongue of higher ground running out from a hillside or ridge; standing above the ground on either side, it drains and stays dry.

Genji.def: A Japanese era name, 1864-1865. The great fire of Genji burned much of Kyoto in the summer of 1864.

back-to-back drain.def: The open drain running down the middle of a block, where the back lots of the houses facing two parallel streets meet; in a castle town it often also marks the boundary between wards.

ogashoya.def: A senior headman set over a group of villages, above the ordinary shoya - one of the commoner offices that did the auxiliary work of rule, and so could be granted a warrior's privileges.

sword hunt.def: The state policy that took weapons from farmers, after which carrying a sword became in principle a privilege of the warrior status alone.

purveyor merchant.def: A merchant house licensed to supply a daimyo or the shogunate - one of the commoner groups that could be granted the surname and the sword.

crenel.def: A gap in the top of a parapet, between two raised stretches of wall, through which a defender looks out and shoots; a row of them makes a crenellated parapet, which from above gives a wall-top its toothed edge.

sub-prefect.def: An official of a Chinese prefecture, second to the prefect over it (tongzhi, literally "joint administrator"), who could be put in charge of works such as a county town's walls.

cascade.def: Paddies stepped one below another down a slope, so that water spills from each field into the next one down. A cascade column is one line of them running downhill; a cascade fan is many columns spread across a fan-shaped slope.

yuecheng.def: The walled outer enclosure in front of a Chinese city gate, a kind of barbican; at Xi'an it was the outermost of a gate's works, and its front gate opened onto the drawbridge over the moat.

zhalou.def: The tower over the front gate of a Chinese city gate's outer enclosure. It is named for the drawbridge it controlled: its soldiers raised the bridge with iron chains and ropes when an enemy came.

koguchi.def: A Japanese castle's gateway: a fortified entrance through its line of walls or earthworks, such as the main gate or the back gate. Some were built so the garrison could sally out, and others so they could be sealed off completely.

Hongwu.def: The reign name of the first Ming emperor, 1368-1398; "the twenty-ninth year of Hongwu" is 1396.

rokusai-ichi.def: The Japanese periodic market held six days a month, every five days, on day pairs such as the 1st and 6th; in the Edo period it was the center of a region's trade in Tohoku and Kanto.

ichigami.def: The market god, worshipped where a market was held to keep its trade safe and fair; its body was most often a round natural stone at the roadside, at an edge of the market - a village boundary, a landing, a bridge foot or a crossroads.

machi-kaisho.def: A town ward's own office and meeting place in an Edo-period city, where the townspeople's officials passed on the magistrate's notices and drew up the residents' papers; every ward of a self-governing city like Osaka had one, while in a castle town it was the exception.

otabisho.def: The place where a shrine's portable shrine rests or stays the night during its festival procession, or which the procession sets out to reach - a small shrine, a temporary altar, or the house of the parish's representative.

tsubo-niwa.def: The small garden inside a Japanese town house, about one to two tsubo (6 ft square to 6 by 12 ft), made as if a piece of the house had been cut out, to let light and air into a house hemmed in by its neighbors.

huiguan.def: A Ming and Qing Chinese association's hall, also called a gongsuo: first a place of fellowship and lodging for people from one home region, and for some later an association of the merchants of one trade.

owaiya.def: In the setting, the burakumin whose profession is handling night soil; in Japan the collectors were farmers and, later, commoner dealers.

miaohui.def: The Chinese temple fair: a gathering near a temple for offerings, contests and performances, first on its festivals and later on fixed dates, which took in market trade until it became a form of the market.

ita-bune.def: A flat board, about 70 cm by 150 cm, on which fish were laid out and sold at Edo's fish market.

banta.def: A watchman hired by an Edo-period town or village for the night watch and the fire watch, often living in a hut beside a ward gate; outside Edo most were of hinin status.

tsujiban.def: A guard box at a street crossing, above all in the samurai quarter of a castle town: in Edo a hut about 12 by 9 ft cut into a mansion wall, manned day and night.

Sekai Daihyakka Jiten.def: Heibonsha's World Encyclopedia, a large Japanese general encyclopedia; Kotobank carries its entries beside the smaller Mypedia and Nipponica.

baba.def: A riding ground: a long, narrow strip of level ground, banked and fenced, where samurai trained their horses and practiced archery from the saddle.

jiaochang.def: A Chinese city's drill ground: a walled open field, usually outside a gate, with a reviewing hall and platform, where the garrison drilled and was reviewed.

lower mansion.def: A ruling house's secondary residence, set toward the edge of the castle town - at Kanazawa outside the outer sogamae, beside the temple quarter and the artisans' town - rather than in the inner quarters.

Wakasa.def: An old province on the Sea of Japan coast north of Kyoto, now the southwest of Fukui prefecture.

Kikaijima.def: A small island in the Amami group, south of Kyushu, whose settlements each kept their own customs and, after 1868, their own graveyards.

temple registration.def: The Edo-period system under which every household was registered with a Buddhist parish temple, which vouched that its members were not Christians and kept their funerals and graves.

hikiri-ichi.def: A Japanese periodic market held on fixed days of the month, usually three times a month. It came before the six-day market (rokusai-ichi) and was replaced by it as trade grew.

zaimachi.def: A country town of Edo-period Japan: a built-up town of merchants and craftsmen in the countryside, outside the castle towns. Around Kyoto and Osaka many six-day markets grew into one.

ke.def: A Chinese unit of time, one hundredth of a day, about 14 and a half minutes.

Sui dynasty.def: The Chinese dynasty (581-618) that reunified China and built the capital the Tang took over as Chang'an.

palisade.def: A barrier of upright wooden stakes or timbers set close together; at Suzhou's Pan Gate one stands across the water passage, front and back, beside the sluice gate, to shut boats out.

chome.def: A numbered section of a Japanese street or district: Honcho 1-chome is the first section of Honcho street.

uogashi.def: A kashi (riverbank landing) that holds a fish market, where fish and shellfish landed from boats were wholesaled to ordinary traders; one was found in every part of the country, Edo's at Nihonbashi the best known.

machi-hanare.def: The name used in Shinano and at Tsuruoka and Sakata for an outcaste quarter placed at a castle town's entrance or edge. It is written 町離, which this record reads as "apart from town".

omoteya-zukuri.def: the grander form of the Kyoto town house: a separate shop block at the street, joined to the main house behind by an entrance block, with an open entrance court and a small court on either side of that block.

senzai.def: the planting of a Japanese garden - its shrubs, trees and flowers; in a Kyoto town house, the planting of the back garden behind the main rooms (the zashiki garden).

yamada.def: Literally "mountain paddy": the name used around the old capital, in the Kinki region, for a paddy opened in a small valley among the hills.

sakoda.def: The name used in the Chugoku region of western Japan for a paddy opened along a narrow valley floor.

spoil bank.def: The earth dug out of a ditch, heaped in a low bank along its side; a ditch's two spoil banks widen the strip of ground it takes up.

dock basin.def: An enclosed pool of still water cut back from a waterway into a town, where boats lie out of the current to load and unload.

bill of lading.def: A shipper's written receipt for goods taken aboard a boat, listing the cargo and where it is bound.

mirin.def: A sweet rice wine brewed for cooking and seasoning.

bangumi.def: At Fukui, the ranked companies of middle samurai: company heads, commissioners and retainers of about 100 to 300 koku, each granted a house lot of fixed size by stipend.

kochi-seki.def: Fukui's highest retainer rank: 17 houses of 1,000 to 4,025 koku, from which the house elders and the castle warden came.

koke.def: At Fukui, a rank of two houses with small stipends but treated as a class apart from the ranks around them.

jozabangai-seki.def: A Fukui middle-samurai rank of about 200 to 450 koku, held by posts such as escort heads and the temple-and-shrine commissioners.

uchibori.def: The innermost of a castle's rings of moats, the one nearest its center. At a flatland castle the outer ring is the sotobori and the ring between the two is the naka-bori.

Shoho.def: A Japanese era name. Its first year, Shoho 1, is 1644, the year the shogun Iemitsu ordered the daimyo of the whole country to make plans of their castles.

fudai.def: A hereditary vassal house of the shogun; the fudai domains are the lands such houses held, set apart from the domains of the lords outside that inner circle.

House Chancellery.def: The domain's governing council; it has no compound of its own and meets in a room of the goten, the daimyo's residence inside the castle.

tsukiyama.def: A Japanese garden built around an artificial mound or small hill (the word means "built mountain"), usually with stones and plantings on and around it - the usual form of a samurai house's garden.

nukimon.def: The simplest framed gate: two posts joined by a horizontal tie-beam (*nuki*) passed through them, with no roof.

azezukuri.def: Bund-making: the yearly rebuilding of a paddy's bunds before the field is flooded, named beside azenuri as the same spring repair (research/archetypes, question 070 notes).

doro-aze.def: "Mud bund": a Japanese name for the earth ridge around a paddy, the same thing as a bund (research/archetypes, question 070 notes).

valley fan.def: Paddies laid out down a valley floor in rows that follow constant-fall contours. Each sector of the fan is a run of rows between a head row, which takes water from the supply canal through cuts in its own bund, and a closing rank on the drain (research/archetypes, question 070).

ring canal.def: The canal that runs around a polder block beside its dike, carrying the block's water around its edge (research/archetypes, question 070).

domain era.def: The period when Japan was governed through the lords' domains (han), roughly 1600-1868; the source cited here dates the opening of most paddies to it (research/archetypes, question 070, `kato-1999-ittanbu-kukaku`).

hyakushodai.def: An Edo-period village officer who spoke for the ordinary farming households, one of the three village offices beside the nanushi (headman) and the kumigashira.

nuptiality.def: A demographer's word for marriage as a measured rate: what share of a population married, and at what age.

matoi.def: The standard of an Edo-period fire company, carried to a fire and held up on the roofs by its bearer. It was kept with the rest of the fire gear in a ward's watch house.

tobiguchi.def: An Edo-period fire hook, used to pull down the houses downwind of a fire so that it could not spread. It was kept with the fire gear in a ward's watch house.

ryudosui.def: The hand pump of an Edo-period fire company. Since fires were fought by pulling houses down, it was mostly used to spray the men on the roofs and shield them from sparks.

genba.def: A carrying bucket, one of the pieces of fire gear an Edo-period ward kept in its watch house.

kichin.def: The firewood fee (木賃, "wood price") an inn charged for cooking the food its guest had brought - the fee that gave the kichin-yado its name.

mushukunin.def: A person off the population register (無宿人, "without a lodging") - with day laborers, the typical lodger packed into a kichin-yado's shared room.

bobana.def: The spot at the edge of an Edo-period post town, on the highway (棒鼻), where the lowest-grade inns stood.

clapper-board.def: A wooden board hung up at a watch post or fire tower and struck with a mallet to raise an alarm or give a signal; the Japanese bangi.

Imperial Magistrate.def: The Emperor's own officer resident in a domain's capital, whose walled compound is the Emperor's ground inside the domain rather than the domain's own; the setting's budget notes fund it at 700 koku a year.

Emerald Charter.def: The Emperor's charter under which each domain receives an Imperial Magistrate, an Imperial samurai appointed from outside the domain and stationed at its capital with their own staff, court and budget.

hectare.def: A metric unit of area: 10,000 square meters, about 107,600 square feet or 2.5 acres.

three arresting tools.def: The three long-handled tools a watch post kept for taking a man alive without cutting him down: a barbed sleeve-catcher, a forked pole and a T-headed push-pole.

ubusuna.def: The god of the place where a person was born. By the Edo period it was treated as the same god as a village's ujigami and chinju.

ubuko.def: Those born under an ubusuna god's protection, who owe it worship. It pairs with the ubusuna the way ujiko pairs with ujigami.

Bingo.def: An old province on the Inland Sea coast of western Honshu, roughly today's eastern Hiroshima prefecture.

Sanuki.def: An old province in northeastern Shikoku, facing the Inland Sea, roughly today's Kagawa prefecture; its plain is one of Japan's named regions of dispersed villages.

Setouchi.def: The lands around the Seto Inland Sea, between western Honshu, Shikoku and northern Kyushu.

shitomi.def: A lattice-faced wooden shutter hinged at the top: it swings up and outward and is hooked open, and in bad weather it closes the opening like a wall panel.

Ashina.def: A warrior house, once lords of Aizu, that held Kakunodate under the Satake lords of Akita from 1620 until its line died out in the 1650s; the Iwahashi family were among its senior retainers.

banner.def: One of the Eight Banners, the hereditary military divisions of the Qing dynasty. Banner troops and their families were garrisoned across the country, most often in a walled quarter of their own in a corner of a provincial capital.

sakimono-gashira.def: The head of one of a castle town's vanguard foot-soldier companies, a high post for a middle-rank retainer. Fukui had sixteen of them, and the one who held the Kaga-guchi gate had an official residence beside it.

Guangxu era.def: The reign of the Qing emperor Guangxu, 1875-1908. Chinese records date events by the year of the reign, so its eleventh year is 1885.

chancellor.def: In the setting, the member of the domain's House Chancellery who sits for one samurai lineage; a House has about six, each of Rank 11, second only to the daimyo.

cosmopolitan lineage.def: In the setting, a samurai lineage tied to no one province, often raised to reward service to the daimyo - unlike a provincial lineage, which is rooted in its home province and in practice holds its governorship by inheritance.

chuma.def: A packhorse carrying trade of Edo-period Japan, in which one man led three or four horses and carried around 100 kan of goods at a time.

Guangxu.def: The reign era of the Qing dynasty's Guangxu emperor, 1875 to 1908; a count dated to it falls late in the Qing.

Kiangsu.def: The older romanized spelling of Jiangsu, the coastal province of the Lower Yangzi that includes much of Jiangnan; the spelling 1920s-1930s surveys such as Buck's use.

Honan.def: The older romanized spelling of Henan, the province on the middle Yellow River in north China; the spelling 1920s-1930s surveys such as Buck's use.

village grain.def: The loose spacing of a farming village: houses stand apart, each among its own plots, with open field between them rather than walls shared along a street.

yabusame.def: Mounted archery run as a contest: a rider gallops straight down a long, narrow riding ground and shoots at targets from the saddle.

dakyu.def: A ball game played on horseback, one of the arts samurai practiced on a riding ground.

dogata.def: A timber copy of the long eaves of Kyoto's Sanjusangendo hall, built by some great domains to practice the long-shot archery contest; some copied only the highest stretch of the arrow's flight, some the whole length.

origake.def: A cheap practice rig for the long-shot archery contest: ropes strung between pairs of bamboo poles, standing in for the roof the arrows had to pass under.

stem family.def: A household of parents living with one married heir and the heir's children, the other children marrying out or leaving; the ordinary farm household of the later Edo period.

joint household.def: A household holding two or more married couples of the same generation - brothers and their wives, say - under one head.

shumon aratame cho.def: The yearly religious-investigation register of an Edo-period village, listing every household and its members with their ages and relations; historians read household sizes from it. Where a domain kept the head count apart from the religious check, the same kind of register was called the ninbetsu aratame cho, the population-investigation register.

myoshu.def: In the early Edo period, a powerful farmer who held dependent farmers, semi-dependent small farmers and collateral kin under one large household. Those dependents later split off into small farms of their own.

person-year.def: A count that weights each person by the years they appear in a register, so someone recorded for five years counts five times.

placer.def: The part of the map generator that seats farmhouses on the sheet. It must seat between 0.85 and 1.05 occupied farmhouses per declared household, and when it runs short it widens the ground it draws seats from.

Bitchu.def: A province of western Japan on the Inland Sea coast. Its village registers of 1870 are one of the record's sources for household size.

Nihonmatsu.def: A castle town and domain in the Tohoku. The record's figures come from two of its villages, Shimo-Moriya and Niida, in their register of 1862.

Suwa.def: A mountain region of central Japan around Lake Suwa, where the average household halved from about eight in the seventeenth century to about four in the nineteenth.

Shikoku.def: The smallest of Japan's four main islands, on the south side of the Inland Sea.

terakoya.def: An Edo-period writing school where a master taught commoners' children to read, write and reckon; it needed only a master and one room, in his house, the headman's or a temple, not a building of its own.

nokaji.def: A village smith: a maker and mender of farm tools, fishing gear and household tools, working small, as a family, to order for the farmers round about.

kajimachi.def: The smiths' street of a castle town, where the lord settled the town's smiths together; the name survives in town after town.

sishu.def: A Chinese private school for children, often held in a family's ancestral hall between its spring and autumn rites.

tofuya.def: A tofu maker, or the shop where tofu is made; from the seventeenth century it sold over its own counter and through peddlers carrying tubs.

crude drug.def: A medicinal plant, animal or mineral part, dried but otherwise unprocessed, which an apothecary compounded into medicine.

yukaku.def: A licensed pleasure quarter of Edo-period Japan: a district where the authorities gathered the licensed brothels, closed off by a wall, a ditch or a fence and entered by a gate. Besides the three great ones of Edo, Kyoto and Osaka, only twenty-odd places in the country had one.

wazi.def: An entertainment precinct of a Song city, open to all comers, holding performance halls (goulan) among shops, teahouses and wine shops. Also called washe.

okabasho.def: An unlicensed place of prostitution in Edo-period Japan, such as a temple-gate town, as against the walled and licensed pleasure quarter.

anjifang.def: A Song state infirmary for the sick poor, set up early in the Chongning era (1102-1106) in the counties and in every sizable town, run by monks recruited for it.

juyangyuan.def: A Song state poorhouse that housed and fed widows, orphans, the old, the disabled and the destitute, set up early in the Chongning era (1102-1106) in the counties and in every sizable town.

Iyo.def: An old province of Japan on the island of Shikoku, the land of the modern Ehime prefecture.

shogunal village.def: A village in land the shogunate held directly, rather than in a daimyo's domain, its taxes paid to the shogun's own officials.

Onin war.def: The war fought in and around Kyoto at the end of the Muromachi period between an eastern and a western army of lords; the western army's camp ground gave Kyoto's weaving quarter, Nishijin, its name.

cotton beater.def: A craftsman who loosened and cleaned raw cotton by striking it with the string of a large bow, readying it for spinning or for padding bedding and clothes.

kakoigura.def: A storehouse for grain held in reserve against bad harvests, which the Edo shogunate ordered villages to build alongside the gogura in 1790.

penthouse.def: In a building's measurements, a smaller structure raised on its roof (Japanese 塔屋, touya) - in a keep, the upper stories set on top of the main floors, counted apart from the stories above ground.

goyobeya.def: The room where a domain's senior councilors (karo) carried out their duties, in the castle palace and in the domain's Edo mansion alike.

tayu.def: A rank of courtesan in the licensed quarters of Edo-period Japan; the record's Osaka source names the tayu first among Shinmachi's more than 800 courtesans in the 1690s and 1700s.

ohaguro-dobu.def: The ditch that ran around the Yoshiwara quarter of Edo, outside its high wall; together with the wall it shut the quarter off from the town.

Kamigata.def: The Kyoto-Osaka region of central Japan, home of the imperial court and the great merchant city - in Edo-period speech, "the upper parts" as against Edo in the east.

five-household group.def: A group of about five neighboring households in an Edo-period village or ward, answerable together for its members; in the villages it was one of the bodies that fought fire until modern times.

young men's association.def: A village's organized body of its young men, which, with the five-household groups, fought the village's fires until modern times.

Tongdian.def: A Tang encyclopedia of institutions compiled by Du You and finished in 801, whose military books preserve the drill of the Tang armies.

pleasure quarter.def: A district of a town set aside for licensed entertainment - teahouses, entertainers' houses and brothels - often near the port or at the town's edge.

seyakuin.def: An ancient Japanese dispensary, set up at a temple or at court, that gave the sick medicine and treatment; the first were founded at Kofukuji in 723 and in the empress's household in 730.

hidenin.def: An ancient Japanese almshouse, founded beside a dispensary (seyakuin), that cared for the sick, orphans and the poor; one was set up at Kofukuji in 723.

tamahagane.def: The steel a tatara smelt yields from iron sand (satetsu) and charcoal. One smelt burned about 9 t of iron sand and 11 t of charcoal to leave about 2.3 t of it, which is why Japanese steel was scarce and went to blades and tools first.

kyuden.def: "Palace": the word Rokugan puts before the name of a clan's or family's great castle-seat, as in Kyuden Shinjo, the seat of the Shinjo family.

Jiajing.def: The reign name of a Ming emperor, by which the years of his reign were counted, 1522 to 1566; its twentieth year is 1541.

Longqing.def: The reign name of a Ming emperor, by which the years of his reign were counted; its first to fourth years are 1567-1570.

Zhengtong.def: The reign name of a Ming emperor, by which the years of his reign were counted; its fourteenth year is 1449.

Jingtai.def: The reign name of the Ming emperor who followed Zhengtong's capture in 1449; its first year is 1450.

Tumu crisis.def: The Mongol defeat and capture of a Ming emperor at Tumu in 1449, after which the Mongols raided deep into northern China.

ox-shoeing frame.def: A frame in which an ox is held, slung, while it is shod - once a village fixture from Spain to England, called a crush or a trevis in English and a potro de herrar in Spanish.

kabuki.def: Japan's popular stage drama of the Edo period, played by male actors with music and dance in roofed city playhouses such as Edo's three licensed theaters and Osaka's Dotonbori houses.

outer moat.def: The outermost moat of a castle town, the line that marked where the city proper ended; Edo's playhouses were moved in 1842 to land far outside it.

tairo.def: The great elder: the shogunate's highest office, filled only at times and ranking above the Roju, with whom its holder sat in Edo castle's goyobeya to run the government.

wakadoshiyori.def: The shogunate's junior elders, ranking below the Roju, who shared the goyobeya in Edo castle with them to conduct the business of government.

Enpo era.def: A Japanese era, 1673 to 1681, the decade of the first count of Osaka's domain kurayashiki.

domain kiln.def: A kiln a domain owned and ran for its own fine ware, kept apart from the ordinary potters - the Nabeshima moved theirs to Okawachiyama in 1675 and set a barrier around it so its techniques and craftsmen could not leave.

Pingyao.def: A walled county town in Shanxi, northern China, whose Ming-dynasty city wall still stands almost entire, its projecting towers at measured intervals.

legibility floor.def: The smallest width a line is drawn at on the map so that it stays visible, even where the real thing is narrower; building footprints get no such allowance and are drawn at their real size.

Grand Canal.def: The canal running north to south through eastern China, from Beijing to Hangzhou; by the Wanli era seven of the eight Ming customs barriers that were kept stood along it.

mural tower.def: A tower built into the run of a city wall, standing out from its face so that defenders can shoot along the wall's foot, as distinct from a gate tower over an opening.

enemy tower.def: A roofed tower built on top of a mamian platform on a Chinese city wall, from which defenders shoot along the wall's face to reduce the ground they cannot hit.

through-lane.def: A lane that runs on through a block or town from one road to another; a side lane that reaches it ends there instead of crossing it.

kara-hafu.def: a Japanese gable whose edge rises in a curve to a peak at its center, built over the gates and entrances of houses of rank.

program item.def: An institution a settlement of a given tier holds exactly one of whatever its size - an item on the list of what that tier contains - as against a building whose number is worked out from the settlement's population.

military examination.def: The Chinese state's examination for military degrees. Under the Ming and the Qing it ran at three levels: provincial, metropolitan (held at the capital) and palace, which was held in the palace with the emperor examining in person.

kizuma.def: A fence of stacked firewood built under a farmstead's windbreak grove on its northwest side, sometimes roofed with straw, that stored the winter fuel and kept off wind and snow - a form of the Isawa plain in Iwate.

nodame.def: A field pit: a night-soil pit set out beside a household's fields or by a road, away from the house, where night soil was kept until it went on the crop.

silver carp.def: A pond fish that feeds on the fine matter in the water; it was fed on dung, whether the livestock's or the grass carp's, so it shared a pond with the grass carp.

nursery pond.def: A pond where fish fry are raised until they are big enough to stock a grow-out pond. In the Pearl River delta only the fry households of Jiujiang kept them; there they took seven parts in ten of the pond water, and a modern manual gives them a quarter to three tenths of a self-stocking farm's pond area.

memorial.def: A written petition an official sent to the emperor to ask for a ruling or an action. To memorialize was to submit one; Liu Daxia's memorial of the Hongzhi reign asked that the West River fry landings be granted to the people of Jiujiang.

four domestic carps.def: The four carps that Chinese pond farmers raised together, each feeding at its own depth: black carp, grass carp, silver carp and bighead carp. From the mid-Ming on, their fry for the delta's ponds came from the West River by way of Jiujiang.

are.def: A metric unit of land area, 100 square meters (about 1,076 sq ft); Japanese farm figures are given per ten ares, about 10,760 sq ft.

barrel coffin.def: A round wooden tub, like a small barrel, in which a commoner's body was buried sitting up - the usual coffin of Edo-period townspeople, cheaper than a long box coffin.

inter.def: To bury; here, to place the ashes left by cremation in a grave, as in the Japanese practice of cremating the dead and then burying a household's urns together in one family plot.
