charity graveyard.def: In Qing China, a burial ground bought and endowed by a donor for the dead no family would bury - the unclaimed, the poor, the drowned of a flood - and packed with coffins. Those in Jiangnan ranged from 3 fen to 10 mu.

drum tower.def: A tower at the central crossing of a Chinese walled city's gate-to-gate streets, where a drum was beaten to mark the hours.

Tsinan.def: The older spelling of Jinan, the provincial capital of Shantung (now spelled Shandong) in northern China; its walled city enclosed the Ta-ming Hu, a lake covering about a fifth of the walled area.

department capital.def: The walled seat of a Chinese department, the administrative rank between the prefecture and the county; its walls were built to enclose less ground than a prefectural city's and more than a county seat's.

J-STAGE.def: Japan's national online library of scholarly journals, where many Japanese academic articles are published as PDFs.

outer town.def: The part of a castle town lying beyond its inner core around the castle; at Sumoto a street lined by a lower mansion and its retainers' houses ran through it.

Court of the Imperial Stud.def: A Ming and earlier Chinese government office in charge of the state's horses: their breeding, pasturing and supply.

Yamakawa Nihonshi Shojiten.def: A concise Japanese dictionary of Japanese history, published by Yamakawa; one of the dictionaries whose entries Kotobank prints.

Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei.def: A large Japanese dictionary of historical place names, with entries down to single towns, districts and streets; Kotobank prints parts of it.

gate paddy.def: The paddy and dry fields at a medieval Japanese resident lord's gate. They belonged to the lord's moated seat, and the moat that defended the house also watered them.

eight trigrams.def: The eight three-line figures of Chinese divination, each set at a compass position and linked to an element such as wind or water; house siting used them to judge which side of a compound was auspicious for its gate.

xun.def: The trigram of wind, set at the southeast; in a courtyard house, the auspicious position for the main gate, letting in the mild southeast wind and shutting out the northwest wind of winter.

Nichō-ibi.def: The outlet sluice at Okinohata, at the seaward end of Yanagawa's canals. It is opened when the castle-town moat is drained, letting the moat's stored water out to the Ariake Sea.

Sengoku house.def: The lords of Ueda domain, a family whose name is written 仙石. The name sounds the same as the Sengoku age of civil wars but is a different word.

Chenghua.def: The reign era of the Ming emperor Xianzong, 1465-1487; a year was dated by counting from its start, so its sixteenth year is 1480.

Siberian high.def: The great mass of cold, heavy air that settles over Siberia in winter. Wind blows out of it over Japan from the northwest all winter; in summer the wind comes from the Pacific instead, from the southeast.

fumoto.def: In Satsuma's outer-district system, the settlement in each of the domain's outer districts where its rural samurai (gōshi) lived, farming in peacetime and serving under the district steward when fighting broke out.

detached territory.def: A domain's lands lying apart from its main territory, often at some distance, and run from a small seat of their own.

underdrainage.def: Drainage laid under a field's soil, as buried pipes or covered channels, that carries off the water standing in a poorly drained field so a wet paddy can be dried between crops.

oroshi.def: A cold wind blowing down off a mountain range onto the plain below in winter; in Japan it is named for the mountain it comes from, like the Zao oroshi of the Sendai plain.

kuchimai.def: A small rice surcharge collected with the land tax, which at first paid for an intendant's office.

hikioi.def: An intendant's debt to the shogunate for tax he had collected and spent rather than passed on.

rice-transit town.def: A town where tax rice from many counties is gathered and forwarded toward the domain or the capital, and that keeps its own row of storehouses to hold it, separate from the magistrate's compound.

kuchiei.def: The coin counterpart of kuchimai: a small surcharge collected with any annual tax assessed in coin rather than rice, and used, like kuchimai, for the intendant's office.

Gofukumachi.def: A castle-town ward of dry-goods (kimono cloth) merchants, named for their trade like other castle-town wards.

Aburayamachi.def: A castle-town ward of lamp-oil sellers, named for their trade like other castle-town wards.

Daikumachi.def: A castle-town ward of carpenters, named for their trade like other castle-town wards.

Kon'yamachi.def: A castle-town ward of indigo dyers, named for their trade like other castle-town wards.

sovereign temple.def: The head temple of a temple order, standing in a domain's capital and run by a Grand Abbot; the order's temples in the provincial cities are subordinate to it. A capital's two sovereign temples on these maps are those of the ruling clan's two patron Fortunes.

Pingjiang tu.def: The 1229 plan of Suzhou, then called Pingjiang, showing the broad moat outside the city wall joined through the water gates to the canals inside it.

nanmu.def: A Chinese evergreen hardwood tree (楠木), one of the hardy trees, with red chinquapin and bamboo, planted in the fengshui grove behind a Hakka enclosed house to hold the soil and water and block the wind.

chinquapin.def: An evergreen tree of the chestnut family; the red chinquapin is one of the hardy trees, with nanmu and bamboo, planted in the fengshui grove behind a Hakka enclosed house to hold the soil and water and block the wind.

Kazusa.def: An old province of Japan on the Boso peninsula, east of Edo Bay, in what is now central Chiba prefecture.

mizunara.def: A Japanese oak that, together with konara, made up most of Nagano's old fuel and charcoal woods, which were cut and let regrow from the stump.

litchi.def: A southern Chinese fruit tree, grown with the longan among a village's houses as dooryard fruit; its small round fruit has a rough red skin and sweet white flesh.

Bizen.def: An old province of Japan on the Inland Sea coast, in what is now the southeastern part of Okayama prefecture.

Mimasaka.def: An old inland province of Japan, north of Bizen, in what is now the northern part of Okayama prefecture.

Awa.def: The name of two old provinces of Japan: Awa (阿波) on Shikoku, now Tokushima prefecture, across the mountains from Sanuki; and Awa (安房) at the southern tip of the Boso peninsula, now part of Chiba prefecture.

Hoki.def: An old province of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast, in what is now the western part of Tottori prefecture.

Inshu.def: Inaba province, the old province whose castle town was Tottori, the domain of the Ikeda family.

thalweg.def: The line of deepest, fastest water along a river channel (Japanese mio-suji). A natural intake sets its mouth on the bank the thalweg runs along, and a crib weir's removable upper frame stood over it.

toshuko.def: Japanese for head works: originally the whole series of works for taking irrigation water from a river - the weir, the intake mouth, the settling basin, the division works - and in later use chiefly the intake weir itself.

Lingqu.def: An ancient Chinese canal joining the Xiang River to the Li River; a pointed divider, the plowshare snout, splits the Xiang so that seven parts of its water return to the Xiang and three pass into the canal.

Ishi-ibi.def: A stone intake sluice in Japan, begun in 1615, whose weir and deflecting works turned the river's flow toward the sluice to take irrigation water, returning the surplus to the main river.

stoplog gate.def: A gate made of timbers laid one on another in grooves across an opening in a weir or sluice; lifting the timbers out lets flood water and sediment through.

fish mouth.def: The pointed head of the dividing levee at Dujiangyan, which splits the river into the inner river, feeding the irrigation channels, and the outer river, carrying the flood.

Wang Zhen.def: A Yuan-dynasty Chinese official whose agricultural treatise, the Nong Shu (1313), describes and illustrates farm tools and irrigation works.

Xiang River.def: A river of south China flowing north through Dongting Lake to the Yangtze; the Lingqu canal takes three parts of its water across to the Li River.

Li River.def: A river of south China flowing south toward the Pearl River; the Lingqu canal joins it to the Xiang River.

Kodera site.def: An excavated Japanese site (古照遺跡) where a weir of slanted stakes and logs was found, built up into A-frames, tied with wisteria vine and packed with clay and gravel.

concave bank.def: The outer bank of a river bend, where the current runs deep and wears the bank away; silt settles on the opposite, inner bank.

grave goods.def: Objects buried with the dead for their use after death; Han-dynasty tombs held pottery models of farm buildings, such as a pigsty with a latrine built above it.

overflow dam.def: A low dam built across a river channel so that the water spills over its top while the level behind it rises high enough to flow into a canal; the Chinese name for what the record elsewhere calls a weir.

pigsty-privy.def: A Chinese farmstead arrangement where the privy is built above the pigsty, so the household's waste and the pigs' dung go into the same manure.

jar burial.def: A burial in which the body is placed in a large pottery jar, sometimes set inside a wooden chamber; one of the grave forms excavated at Edo temple graveyards.

Sensoji.def: The great Buddhist temple at Asakusa in Edo (Tokyo), the head temple of a group of branch temples.

Yanagita Kunio.def: Japanese scholar (1875-1962) who founded the study of Japanese folklore; he recorded village customs across the country.

feather.def: In a map's drawing, the soft edge of a band of marks, which thins out gradually over a strip instead of stopping at a line - as a marsh's reeds do inside its boundary.

Ussuriland.def: The region of the Russian Far East along the Ussuri River, east of Manchuria and north of Korea. Red pine reaches the edge of its range there and is rare.

taper law.def: The rule by which a drawn channel narrows from its head to its tail, so that the two ends of one canal differ in width.

weblio.def: A Japanese online dictionary site that gathers entries from many published dictionaries and glossaries under one search; the record uses it, like kotobank, to check whether a Japanese term has a dictionary entry.

Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism.def: The school of Confucian learning founded by the Song-dynasty scholars Cheng Hao, Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi. It stressed family and clan ritual and was the state orthodoxy of late imperial China.

major axis.def: The longest dimension of a grave, coffin or burial chamber, its length, as an excavation report measures it.

rotation period.def: The years a grave is held before its ground is reused for another burial.

gazetted.def: Officially designated by notice in a government gazette - of a forest or reserve, put under legal protection as a named protected area.

slope face.def: The sloping earthen side of a bund or of a terraced field, falling from the field's edge to the ground below. It cannot be cropped and is kept cut like the bund top; in mountain paddies it can cover more ground than the flooded field above it.

commons.def: Land a village held and used in common for firewood, brush and dry grass, lying beyond the protected grove on the high side.

red pine.def: The Japanese red pine, a hardy pine that took over village hills stripped of their broadleaf wood; red pine stands lie between grass hill and bare ground.

bald hill.def: A hill stripped of its trees and brush down to bare ground by overcutting for fuel, common in Japan by the Edo period.

closed-canopy.def: Of a wood whose tree crowns meet overhead, so that little light reaches the ground.

montane.def: Of the mountains: belonging to the higher slopes above a valley.

anthropogenic.def: Caused by human activity - here, plant cover cut, burned or grazed by villagers rather than left to grow.

Heisei.def: The name of Japan's imperial era from 1989 to 2019, used for dating and in the titles of national selections made during those years.

floating-leaf plant.def: A water plant rooted in the pond bed whose leaves float flat on the surface - hishi (water chestnut), asaza (fringed water lily), lotus. In a pond's zonation it grows beyond the emergent reed belt, in deeper water, with the submerged plants further out still.

Blyxa.def: A small submerged water plant of ponds and paddies (Japanese subuta). It is endangered and in marked decline nationwide, and it survives mostly in small, still-managed tameike.

Ottelia.def: A water plant of ponds and paddies (Japanese mizu-oobako) that roots in the bed under shallow water. It is endangered and in marked decline nationwide, and it survives mostly in small, still-managed tameike.

hotoke.def: A buddha, or any deity of Buddhist worship, set beside the kami of Shinto; a shrine or temple may enshrine either.

Yamanote.def: The JR Yamanote line, the railway loop around central Tokyo; "inside the Yamanote loop" means the city's core.

break of slope.def: A line where a slope's steepness changes: the lower break is the concave bend at the slope's foot, the upper break the convex bend at its top.

meisho zue.def: An Edo-period illustrated gazetteer of famous places, whose bird's-eye pictures of shrines, temples and scenery were sketched from life.

ichimoji-zeki.def: In the Edo period, a weir built straight across a river, square to its flow. The name means "the character for one", a single straight stroke. It is shorter than a slanting minote-zeki.

minote-zeki.def: In the Edo period, a weir built slanting with the river's flow and longer than a straight ichimoji-zeki. Its intake is on the downstream side, the side toward which the water flows.

underflow.def: Water that runs underground through a riverbed's or a fan's gravels instead of on the surface (伏流, fukuryu). On an alluvial fan it sinks at mid-fan, leaving the streams there dry, and comes back up as springs at the fan's toe.

water table.def: The depth below the ground surface at which the soil is saturated with groundwater. Where it is deep, as across an alluvial fan's mid-fan, paddy is hard to water and crops needing little water, such as mulberry, were grown instead.

deep percolation.def: Irrigation water that sinks below the reach of the crop's roots and joins the groundwater. It is lost to the field but recharges the ground below, and it can raise the water table enough to waterlog it.

fukuro-zeki.def: In the Edo period, a weir whose middle sags downstream, so that the sand coming down the river settles in that pocket instead of burying the intake. It was used on rivers carrying much sand.

evapotranspiration.def: The water a flooded field loses to the air - by evaporation from the water and soil and by transpiration through the rice plants' leaves - counted with what seeps down as the daily loss the supply must make good.

meso scale.def: In a study of land by spatial scale, the middle scale: a district, between the whole region and a single site. The Tokyo shrine-grove survey's meso scale is the ground inside the Yamanote loop, between all 23 wards and single shrines.

Kanto school.def: The older Edo practice of water management on the Kanto plain, which ran irrigation and drainage in the same channels, so that securing water downstream made drainage difficult upstream; the Kishu school, brought there in the 1720s, separated them.

ren.def: A classical Chinese measure of depth or height, 7 or 8 chi by different commentators.

Lacey.def: Gerald Lacey's regime rule: an empirical law, drawn from stable earthen irrigation canals, that ties a channel's wetted perimeter, width and depth to the water it carries - the perimeter and width growing as the square root of the discharge.

Jomon period.def: Japan's prehistoric age of hunter-gatherers and pottery that came before the Yayoi period; rice paddies first appear toward its end.

Jiangren.def: In the Rites of Zhou's craft chapter (the Kaogongji), the builders - the office that laid out and dug the field channels, from the one-chi quan up to the hui that runs into the rivers.

micro-high ground.def: Ground a little higher than the low-lying plain around it, such as the raised strip beside a river; a canal cut along it can send its water down onto the lower land.

Suiren.def: In the Rites of Zhou, the officer over the outer districts of the royal domain, whose chapter lays out their grain land and its ladder of channels.

senkomizu.def: Timing each turn at the irrigation water by how long a fixed number of incense sticks takes to burn; used where severe drought forced some paddies to be planted with dry field crops instead.

San'in.def: The Sea of Japan coast of western Honshu, a country of deep snow where the weather changes easily at harvest.

Hokuriku.def: The Sea of Japan coast of central Honshu, north of the Kinki, a country of deep winter snow.

Tokai.def: The Pacific coast of central Honshu, between the Kanto and the Kinki, along the Tokaido road.

senbakoki.def: The threshing comb of the Edo period: a row of long iron teeth set in a frame, through which the cut rice was drawn a handful at a time to strip the grain; it replaced threshing chopsticks.

Musashino.def: The broad upland plateau of Musashi province west of Edo, settled in the Edo period by new-field villages laid out in rows, whose dry fields grew barley, millets and vegetables.

gou.def: In the Rites of Zhou's scheme for laying out the countryside, the channel serving ten farmers' allotments; it has a field road on it.

xu.def: In the Rites of Zhou's scheme for laying out the countryside, the channel serving a hundred farmers' allotments; it has a lane on it.

kuai.def: In the Rites of Zhou's scheme for laying out the countryside, the channel serving a thousand farmers' allotments; it has a road on it. Above it only the river remains.

Taiko survey.def: The land survey that Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the Taiko, carried out across Japan in the 1580s and 1590s. It replaced the older great, half and small units of area with the tan of 300 bu.

sui channel.def: In the Rites of Zhou's scheme for laying out the countryside, the smallest channel, the one between two farmers' allotments; it has a path along it.

komatsuna.def: A Japanese leafy green of the mustard family, grown for its leaves and eaten cooked or pickled; it does with half a day of sun.

negi.def: The Japanese long green onion, a bunching onion grown for its long white-and-green stalk; it does with half a day of sun.

mitsuba.def: A Japanese herb, sometimes called Japanese wild parsley, grown for its three-part leaves; it grows even in shade.

myoga.def: A Japanese ginger grown for its edible flower buds and shoots; it grows even in shade.

shiso.def: Perilla, a leaf herb of the mint family grown for its fragrant leaves; it grows even in shade.

proso.def: A small-grained millet (Japanese kibi), grown as a summer grain on dry fields.

foxtail millet.def: A millet (Japanese awa) with a dense, drooping, bristly seed head, one of the chief grains of premodern dry fields.

seed drill.def: A sowing tool drawn by an ox that drops seed through its hollow legs into the soil in straight rows. The Qimin yaoshu names a two-legged one.

Hou Ji.def: The legendary first farmer of Chinese tradition, honored as the founder of grain growing and the ancestor of the Zhou royal house.

fuki.def: Japanese butterbur, a shade-tolerant plant of damp ground whose long leaf stalks are cooked as a vegetable.

seri.def: Japanese water dropwort, a creeping herb of wet ground and paddy margins, eaten as a spring green.

shungiku.def: Garland chrysanthemum, a leafy green whose young leaves are eaten boiled or in hot pots.

Double Ninth.def: The festival of the ninth day of the ninth month of the old calendar, when chrysanthemums were shown and viewed; the Japanese court kept it until the Meiji period, and it lives on as an imperial garden party.

low-trunk mulberry.def: Mulberry trained on a short trunk, cut back lower than mid-trunk mulberry but above the ground where root-cut bushes are cut. In the Taihu district it came into use after mid-trunk mulberry had spread from the Ming dynasty on.

courtesy name.def: A second name a Chinese man took at adulthood and was addressed by in place of his given name; Xu Guangqi's was Zixian.

Dejima.def: A small artificial island in Nagasaki harbor, the one port where Dutch traders were allowed to trade with Japan during the Edo period.

free stall.def: In modern cattle housing, a single stall that an untied animal walks into to lie down and leaves at will, sized to one beast - the FAO manual gives 2.2 m by 1.2 m for a cow of 500 to 600 kg.

Restoration.def: The change of government in 1868 that ended the Edo period and the rule of the shoguns and began the Meiji years.

Tangible Cultural Property.def: A building or object entered on Japan's national register of cultural properties; the register's pages give each building's date, construction and size.

Ubame.def: One of the county manors drawn for this project, beside Ochiba and Hayakawa: a border magistracy of about 290 by 200 ft whose east wall is the line between two clans' lands, with a parley room built into it.

hanebashi.def: A Japanese cantilever bridge with no pier: timbers set into holes in the bank rock on both sides, each layer projecting a little further over the water, with the deck laid across their ends.

carried deck.def: a bridge deck borne on girders across the water, as against a standalone footplank whose ends simply rest on the bank; its corners must all land on dry ground, about 10 ft past the water.

substructure.def: the part of a bridge below its deck and beams - its abutments at the ends and any piers between - that carries them down to the ground.

reaction.def: in engineering, the force a support pushes back with where a beam rests on it - equal to the load the beam puts on that support, and what sizes the beam's bearing seat.

out-to-out.def: of a length, measured from the outer face at one end to the outer face at the other - a beam's whole length, including the parts resting on its supports.

Jingshi fangxiang zhi.def: A late-Qing record of the lanes and wards of Beijing ("the capital"). A modern writer takes from it the count of 1,228 wells across Beijing's inner and outer cities at the end of the Qing.

Ouchi.def: A warrior house of the Muromachi period whose residence stood at Yamaguchi, in western Japan; its excavated residence site is a source for wells of that period.

three-worlds-myriad-spirits.def: A stone or small tower inscribed to the spirits of all beings in the three Buddhist realms (desire, form and formlessness), set up at the entrance of a graveyard or temple as a memorial for all the dead - the known and the unknown alike - and one of the Edo-period graveyard's representative stone monuments, beside the six jizo.

suji-bei.def: A temple's earthen wall striped with white horizontal lines (jōgi-suji), whose number, five the highest, showed the temple's rank.

Shinden Togashi.def: The Dragon Clan's mountain temple city in this setting, a large city whose pilgrims at any time outnumber its natives.

variety hall.def: A small hall in Edo-period towns where paying audiences heard storytellers and other popular entertainers - one of the customer trades that set salt at its doorway.

paper ingot.def: Paper folded or cut into the shape of a gold or silver ingot, burned at a grave as money for the dead; in 1630s Beijing families burned them at the grave on Qingming day and then set paper money on the grave's top.

hōin.def: "Seal of the Law" - the highest of the three honorary ranks of a Buddhist priest.

Wakamiya.def: A shrine to the "young prince" - the offspring, or newly invoked spirit, of a main shrine's deity - often a subsidiary shrine standing in or near the main one's precinct.

Myōken.def: The bodhisattva of the Pole Star and the Big Dipper, worshipped at temples and shrines named for it; Myōkenzan at Kudamatsu is one such mountain cult.

sōzu.def: The middle of the three official ranks of the Buddhist priesthood, below sōjō and above risshi; an "acting" (gon) sōzu held the grade just under the full one.

aragaki.def: One of the fences round a shrine: a tale of 1283 names it with the tamagaki and the mizugaki as the layers of fence that enclosed a great shrine's sanctuary.

Kojiki.def: A book of Japan's myths and early history, finished in 712. Its songs give the earliest written uses of some Japanese words, among them tamagaki, the word for a shrine's fence.

yorigumi.def: A rank of retainers of the Mori family's Hagi domain; the Kuchiba family, at 1,018 koku, held it at the end of the Edo period.

haikai.def: Linked comic verse, the popular form of Japanese linked poetry in the Edo period, from which the haiku later grew.

senryu.def: A short comic verse in the same seventeen-syllable form as the haiku, about everyday life and human failings, much written in the Edo period.

Nihon Dai-hyakka Zensho.def: A Japanese general encyclopedia, one of the reference works whose entries Kotobank carries.

Zhengde.def: The reign name of a Ming dynasty emperor, by which years in China were counted; Zhengde 14 is 1519.

kannon-biraki.def: A pair of door leaves that meet in the middle and swing open to either side, like the doors of a shrine cabinet - the kind of plastered double doors that close a storehouse's doorway.

namako-tiled.def: A wall facing of square flat tiles whose joints are raised in thick white plaster, used on a storehouse's lower walls against rain and fire.

yokogi.def: A crosspiece struck in sword practice: in a branch line of Satsuma swordsmanship, a bundle of a dozen or more long thin branches laid at knee height and struck with a wooden sword.

Shimazu.def: The warrior house that ruled the Satsuma domain.

dou.def: In the Pearl River delta, a sluice through a polder's dike, through which the polder's land and ponds were watered and drained.

fish-scale register.def: A Chinese land register of the Ming and Qing, listing every numbered parcel of a district, polder by polder, with its area and holder.

Pan Jixun.def: A Ming official who ran the Yellow River and Grand Canal works and wrote a manual of them, the Hefang yilan.

lying willow.def: A low willow planted densely from walnut-thick cuttings close to a dike's foot, with only a few cun showing above ground, so its branches and leaves fend off wind and waves; Pan Jixun's Ming river manual pairs it with the long willow.

long willow.def: A tall willow set about 5-6 chi out from a dike, which holds back the water and each year gives big branches for fascines; Pan Jixun's Ming river manual pairs it with the lying willow.

yu.def: Fei Xiaotong's word for a Lake Tai polder: a block of fields enclosed by a dike, whose raised margin carried the mulberry trees and the houses.

juan.def: One of the numbered books a Chinese work is divided into, like a volume or chapter.

sheng.def: A Chinese unit of grain volume, a tenth of a dou; ten he make one sheng.

Lu Guimeng.def: A poet whose poems describe the farm landscape around Lake Tai; reports on the region's dike-ponds still quote them.

Nongzheng Quanshu.def: The "Complete Treatise on Agricultural Administration", Xu Guangqi's compendium of Chinese farming and water management, compiled in the late Ming and printed in 1639.

JA.def: Japan Agricultural Cooperatives, Japan's national federation of farmers' cooperatives; "JA Iwakuni" is its local cooperative for the Iwakuni area.

Amoy.def: The older Western name of Xiamen, a port on the Fujian coast of southeast China.

deep-water lotus.def: Lotus grown for its root in standing water, in a village's lowest and wettest plots - the older form in China, essentially the only one grown before the Song dynasty, when shallow-water lotus first appears in the texts.

shallow-water lotus.def: Lotus grown for its root in shallower water than deep-water lotus - first recorded in China in Song-dynasty texts.

water caltrop.def: An aquatic plant grown in lakes and ponds for its horned, starchy nut (Chinese 菱, ling) - one of the water vegetables of the lake districts around Suzhou.

water shield.def: A floating-leaved pond plant (Chinese 莼菜, chuncai) whose young jelly-coated leaves are eaten as a vegetable - a water vegetable of Taihu's lake districts.

foxnut.def: The seed of a prickly water lily (Chinese 芡实, qianshi), gathered from lakes and ponds and eaten as a starchy food.

wild-rice stem.def: The swollen stem of a wild rice grass (Chinese 茭白, jiaobai), grown in shallow water and eaten as a vegetable.

Water Margin.def: A Chinese novel of the Ming dynasty about a band of outlaws, set in the Northern Song; one chapter describes an army fodder depot.

Koeki Kokusanko.def: A Japanese farm book of the late Edo period; among much else it describes the kunugi cut for Ikeda charcoal.

daiba kunugi.def: A kunugi oak cut back at a height of about a meter or more, so that many thin branches sprout from the stump and can be cut again every several years for charcoal.

makusa.def: An old Japanese reading of 秣, one of the two old characters for fodder, as the Wamyo Ruijusho gives it; the other, 蒭, it reads karakusa, "dried grass".

Hexi Corridor.def: The long, narrow strip of oases in the northwest of China through which the Han road ran west to Dunhuang; the Han post station of Xuanquanzhi stood in its desert.

Sagamino.def: The Sagami plain, the upland of central Sagami province (today's Kanagawa), southwest of Edo; its villages cut fodder and roofing material on shared ground.

Zama.def: A district on the Sagamino upland in Sagami province (today's Kanagawa), southwest of Edo.

Shanhaiguan.def: The fortified pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, on the road from Korea and Manchuria to Beijing; the Korean embassy of 1780 passed through it on its way to the Qing court.

Jehol.def: Rehe (older spelling Jehol), the Qing emperors' summer residence north of the Great Wall, today Chengde; Park Ji-won's Jehol Diary is his account of the 1780 Korean embassy that traveled there for the Qianlong Emperor's seventieth birthday.

Tartary.def: An old European name for the lands north and west of China proper - Mongolia, Manchuria and Central Asia.

Salt Road.def: The old Japanese road that carried salt inland from the Japan Sea coast to Shinano, today Nagano, much of it on the backs of packhorses and cattle; Otari lies on it.

sapeck.def: The European name for the Chinese copper cash, the smallest coin of Qing China; Huc's Peking night shelter charged one sapeck a night.

phalanstery.def: The great communal building in which the French social theorist Charles Fourier proposed that a whole community live and work together; Huc uses the word in jest of Peking's feather-floored night shelter.

Fourier.def: Charles Fourier (1772-1837), a French social theorist who proposed that communities live together in one great shared building, the phalanstery.

Peking.def: The older European name of Beijing, the capital of the Qing dynasty.

Gyosho.def: One of the editions of Hiroshige's Tokaido print series, known in Japanese as the Gyosho Tokaido (行書東海道); its print of Minakuchi shows a kichin-yado with its name on its paper doors.

Huc.def: Evariste Huc (1813-1860), a missionary who lived in Qing China in the 1840s and wrote an account of the empire, published in French in 1854 and in English in 1855.

Toriimoto.def: A small post town on the Nakasendo in Omi, near Hikone; the shogunate's 1843 survey gave it a street about 1.4 km long and 293 houses.

Nakatsugawa.def: A post town on the Nakasendo in Mino, today in Gifu; its street ran about 1.1 km from 1663 to the end of the shogunate.

Tsumago.def: A small post town on the Nakasendo in the Kiso valley, whose street ran about 270 m through the Edo period.

Xu Tan.def: A Chinese economic historian of the Ming and Qing markets, who estimated the density and reach of China's rural periodic markets in the mid-Qing.

Nakasendo Shukuson Taigaicho.def: The shogunate's survey of the post towns and villages along the Nakasendo, made by the road magistrate in 1841-1844, recording each station's length along the road and its houses.

Raozhou.def: A Ming-Qing prefecture of six counties, one of them the county seat of Leping, whose wall was first built in 1562.

Narai.def: A post town whose Edo-period townscape is preserved today, about 1 km long along the Narai River and 200 m across.

Seki.def: A post town on the Tokaido whose street of Edo-period houses is preserved today as a preservation district.

Leping.def: A county seat in Jiangxi, China, whose walled town and street grid a planning article describes.

zaigomachi.def: A country market town of the Edo period that grew up among the villages as a center of the rural economy, rather than as a castle or post town; in the Kinai around Osaka they formed from the late 17th century, every few kilometers.

gannin.def: An Edo-period mendicant who begged in the streets under a religious guise, handing out riddle slips, singing and dancing through the town; in 1842 the town magistrate's office found them living in a few blocks of Edo, Shitaya Yamazaki-cho among them.

dosō.def: A medieval Japanese moneylender who lent on pledges, called after the large, solid earthen storehouse that held the pledged goods; the Muromachi-period forerunner of the pawnbroker (shichiya).

horse-head wall.def: In a Chinese town building, a high gable wall that rises above the roof at the building's end as a fire wall; the Qinxiang pawnshop's street front had one 8 m high.

treadle pestle.def: A foot-worked grain pounder: the mortar is fixed in the ground and the pestle sits on one end of a see-saw beam, so stepping on the other end and letting go drops the pestle onto the grain. It is how a rice dealer polished brown rice in the shop.

refining forge.def: A forge where raw iron from the smelting furnace is reheated and hammered to drive out its slag and make iron a smith can work. It is a very large fire, but one that is stoked and watched throughout.

Eitaijima.def: An island at Edo onto which the city's timber dealers were gathered after the great fire of 1641, blamed on their high stacks of timber; it was later called Moto-Kiba.

pile.def: A timber post driven upright into a riverbed or soft ground, used alone or in clusters to anchor a boom or carry a structure.

raft-mat.def: A raft of logs lashed together flat and moored against a slack bank or in a pond, the way a premodern East Asian timber city held its stock on the water.

clay mill.def: A hand-turned mill for rice, brought from Qing China in the Genroku era, that stripped the husk from the grain but broke many grains as it did.

yonnomaru.def: The fourth bailey of a castle, lying beyond the sannomaru; Hirosaki Castle had one among its six baileys.

hill-and-plain castle.def: A castle built on a low hill rising from a plain, its inner baileys on the rise and its outer baileys spread over the flat ground around it - a type between the mountain castle and the flat-ground castle.

Special Historic Site.def: The highest grade of Japan's national designation of historic sites, above an ordinary Historic Site, given to those judged of the greatest significance.

duty cycle.def: How much of the time a gate stands open, shut or partway between. A wet moat's gates rest partly raised and are trimmed a few inches, rather than being switched open and shut.

spate.def: A river in flood after heavy rain, running high and carrying a heavy load of silt. Canal and moat intakes were wound down or rested while it lasted.

prefect.def: In imperial China, the official who governed a prefecture and its seat city, including public works such as dredging the city moat.

military commissioner.def: In Song China, a regional official with charge of a frontier circuit's defense and civil affairs (Chinese jinglüe shi). At Guangzhou this included the city's moat.

Rokudō crossroads.def: The crossroads at the entrance to Toribeno, Heian-kyō's cremation ground, held to be the boundary between this world and the other world; funerals sent the dead off from there.

Jogyo hall.def: A Buddhist hall; the one founded in 1667 beside the Kozukappara execution ground was built to bury the dead and hold memorial services for them, and later became Minami-Senju Eko-in.

IFC.def: The International Fire Code, a present-day model fire code used across the United States. The record takes only one figure from it: a bonfire must stand 50 ft (15 m) from a structure or anything that burns.

spotting.def: In a wildfire, new fires started ahead of the main fire by burning fragments that the wind or the fire's own updraft carries there. Only a still-burning fragment starts one more than about 60 m from the main fire.

crown fire.def: A wildfire burning through the tops (the crowns) of trees, not along the ground. It is the fire whose rising column of heat carries burning fragments far enough to start new fires at a distance.

convection column.def: The column of hot air and smoke that rises above a large fire. It lifts burning fragments high enough for the wind to carry them beyond the fire.

firebrand.def: A burning or glowing piece of wood or bark carried off by a fire. Once it lands, only one that is still burning can start a new fire.

Yōrō code.def: The ritsuryo law code compiled in 718 and put into force in 757, Japan's classical code of administration. Its funeral ordinance keeps burial away from the capital and the roads, but it gives no distance.

Suitengu.def: A shrine to a water god in the line of the Suitengu of Kurume, revered for protection against water disasters and for safe birth; the lords of Kurume enshrined it at their Edo residence in 1818, and its faith spread from there.

throw-across weir.def: A weir made of logs laid across a river, with thinner logs, branches and gravel set against them; in a flood the crossing logs are taken out so that the river runs on past the intake instead of breaking its gates and banks. The one at Hamura turns the Tama river into the Tamagawa aqueduct.

harakata-shu.def: Yonezawa's lower samurai, whom the Uesugi house settled on the moors around the town by about 1609 after its fief was cut in 1601. Each was given a lot of about 150 tsubo, and the back half was a vegetable field for growing their own food.

Bunkyu.def: A Japanese era name of the last years of the shogunate (1861-1864); Osaka's "Bunkyu fire" was the city's great fire of 1863.

Shaka Nyorai.def: The historical Buddha, Shakyamuni, in his form as a Tathagata, the Japanese name under which a temple enshrines him as its principal image.

principal image.def: The statue or picture of a buddha or deity that a temple enshrines in its main hall as the chief object of its worship.

thirty guardian deities.def: The thirty kami the Nichiren sect worshipped as protectors of the Lotus Sutra, one on guard for each day of the month. A Nichiren temple might keep a hall to them, as Kōshōji at Senjudō did in 1843, with its own tax-exempt land.

land class.def: The Meiji state's sorting of land, by a decree of 1874, into government land and private land, each in numbered classes that decided whether the land paid land tax. A temple precinct was usually government land class 4 (untaxed); one a temple owned outright was private land.

Rennyo.def: A leader of the Shin sect whose letters to his followers (the Ofumi) are still read. In 1471, at fifty-seven, he moved to Yoshizaki, where a town of priests' lodging houses grew up round his temple.

Ofumi.def: Rennyo's letters to the Shin sect's followers, collected in fascicles. The sect also calls them the Gobunshō.

ujibito.def: At the Kamigamo shrine, the hereditary clan members who served as its priests alongside the shrine officials. Until the Restoration both lived in the shrine's priests' quarter, among farmers.

Daoguang.def: The reign name of the Qing emperor who ruled China from 1821 to 1850. Years are counted from its start, so Daoguang 26 is 1846.

middle rowhouse.def: The rowhouse a lord's men below full samurai rank, down to the foot soldiers, lived in, built in a standard unit of nine shaku by two ken (about 9 by 12 ft): one ken at the entrance an earth floor for taking off shoes, the other a raised plank floor.

Chen Fu.def: A writer of the Song dynasty whose farming manual, completed in 1149, describes the wet-rice farming of the lower Yangtze.

cudrania.def: A thorny tree related to mulberry (Chinese 柘, zhe). Its leaves were fed to silkworms when mulberry leaves ran short, and it was planted on pond banks and field edges beside mulberry.

chuan.def: In the Rites of Zhou's field layout, the largest channel in the series of field channels, serving ten thousand allotments - in effect a river, with a road along its bank.

Man'yoshu.def: The oldest surviving collection of Japanese poetry, put together in the late 8th century.

Heike monogatari.def: A war story of the early 13th century about the wars of the 1180s between the Taira (Heike) and Minamoto clans.

sheet pile.def: A flat board driven edge-down into the ground beside others like it, to make a wall that holds back earth or water.

abatis.def: A barrier of felled trees laid with their branches pointing toward the enemy.

shigarami.def: A row of stakes driven into a river with brushwood or bamboo woven onto them from both sides, to hold back the flow.

Lushi chunqiu.def: A Chinese classic compiled about 239 BC under the Qin chancellor Lü Buwei, whose chapters range over government, ritual and seasonal custom; one argues for modest funerals and says a grave belongs on high ground.

evocation.def: In the commentary on the Book of Songs, the label (Chinese xing) for a poem that opens on an image from nature - here cattail and lotus - before it turns to its subject.

Mao commentary.def: The oldest surviving commentary on the Book of Songs, printed with the poems in the edition this project reads.

Qin.def: The state in northwest China whose king unified China in 221 BC and became its first emperor; "pre-imperial Qin" is that state before the unification.

Kyuyo.def: The official chronicle of the Ryukyu kingdom (球陽), written in classical Chinese and first compiled in the mid-eighteenth century; it records the kingdom's events year by year, among them the moving of villages.

Ryukyu kingdom.def: The kingdom that ruled Okinawa and the islands around it from the fifteenth century until Japan annexed it in 1879; the Satsuma domain controlled it from 1609 while it kept its own king and government.

torreya.def: An evergreen conifer related to the yew, grown in southern China for its edible nuts; at Huangling it stands among the yews, camphors and ginkgos of the water-mouth grove.

five grains.def: The traditional Chinese name for the staple grain crops taken together (the list varies by source, usually millets, wheat, rice, beans and hemp); in a farm manual it means simply "field crops".

hui.def: In the Rites of Zhou's ladder of field channels, the grade above the xu and below the chuan: a crosswise channel laid on the south side for every ten xu, and nine of them make a chuan.

feedlot.def: A modern pen where beef cattle are kept close together and fed to put on weight before slaughter, with water supplied at troughs. The record takes its figures for how fast cattle drink from feedlot studies, as a stand-in for a working ox.

toon.def: A tall tree of China (Toona sinensis), also called Chinese mahogany. Its young shoots are eaten and its reddish timber was valued. It was planted around villages and at their water mouths.

tung.def: A Chinese tree (Vernicia fordii) grown for the oil pressed from its seeds, which was used to waterproof wood, paper and cloth.

brush cutter.def: A hand-held motor mower with a spinning blade or line on a long shaft, used today to cut the grass on bunds and slope faces; a modern, mechanized tool.

collective farm.def: In modern Japan, a farming corporation formed by the households of one hamlet, which pool their fields and farm them together; not a state farm.

clonal.def: Of a bamboo stand: every culm in it grew from one spreading rhizome, so the whole thicket is a single plant with the same genes throughout, and in most cases nearly one species.

mitsumata.def: A shrub (Edgeworthia) grown for its bark, which is pulped to make Japanese paper; the 1910 survey maps give a field of it a symbol of its own.

Rakugai-zu.def: "Scenes outside the capital": a folding screen or picture of the countryside and villages round Kyoto, painted in the early Edo period. It is a companion to the screens that show the city itself.

qiu.def: A Chinese timber tree (楸, a kind of catalpa). The sixth-century farm manual says it has no seed, so it is raised from suckers dug around a grown tree, and spaced like catalpa.

catalpa.def: A broad-leaved tree grown in China for timber. The sixth-century farm manual sets it two paces apart because it must grow large.

thinning.def: Cutting out some of the trees of a young planted wood so the rest have room to grow on. Edo documents say a thick planting could not reach its aim without it.

forest stand.def: A patch of woodland treated as one unit for counting and management, with its trees of about the same age and kind. Foresters give its stems per hectare and its age in years (a "23-year stand").

Hongzhi.def: A reign era of the Ming dynasty, 1488-1505.

fry landing.def: A stretch of West River bank where wild fish fry were netted. From the Hongzhi reign on, these stretches were granted to Jiujiang's fry households, who paid a levy on each every year.

Xuanhu.def: The literary name of Xu Guangqi, compiler of the Nongzheng quanshu. The passages headed "Master Xuanhu says" are his own comments.

Guangdong xinyu.def: New Discourses on Guangdong, the late-Ming and early-Qing Lingnan scholar Qu Dajun's seventeenth-century account of Guangdong: its places, its crafts and its customs.

jin.def: A Chinese unit of weight, the catty: a little over a pound.

integrated fish farming.def: Raising fish in the same farm as livestock or crops, so that the animals' manure and the farm's wastes go into the ponds and feed the fish, usually with pig sheds built on the pond dikes. The name and the manuals that teach it are modern.

Hakata.def: A port town on the north coast of Kyushu, for centuries Japan's harbor for trade with the continent; today part of the city of Fukuoka.

Canton.def: The old European name for Guangzhou, the chief port of the Pearl River delta in south China, and the end of the British embassy's overland journey in 1793-94.

retiring house.def: An old English phrase for a privy: in the 1797 embassy account, a small roadside or village privy whose tank was built so that nothing soaked away, and kept as manure.

Nongshu.def: Wang Zhen's farming book of 1313, a Chinese treatise on agriculture; its chapter on manuring the soil describes brick manure pits at the head of southern fields.

Shen shi nongshu.def: A Ming-dynasty farm manual of the Shen family, which says cattle manure goes into a pit (tan) with water added to rot it, and that the pit must be deep and large.

Huzhou-Jiaxing.def: The silk-raising country on the south side of Lake Tai, named for its two prefectural cities, Huzhou and Jiaxing, in Zhejiang.

Tenmei.def: An era of Japan's Edo period, in the 1780s. The Tenmei famine of that decade was one of the Edo period's three great famines, with Kyoho and Tenpo.

Mutsu.def: An old province of Japan in the far north-east of Honshu, the main island.

Shinano.def: An old province of Japan in the central mountains of Honshu, today's Nagano.

Izumi.def: An old province of Japan on Osaka Bay, south of today's Osaka.

Hizen.def: An old province of Japan in north-western Kyushu, today's Saga and Nagasaki.

Honjo.def: A district of Edo east of the Sumida River, today part of Tokyo's Sumida ward.

common cemetery.def: A cemetery a Japanese city ran for its residents at large, as opposed to a temple's or a household's own ground. In 1930s Tokyo it was where most households interred their cremated remains in a family urn plot.

text layer.def: The machine-read text that a scanned PDF carries beneath its page images, which can be searched and copied. It can misread the scan, so a quotation taken from it is checked against the image.

Mypedia.def: A short Japanese encyclopedia from the publisher Heibonsha, one of the reference works whose entries Kotobank carries.

Shima.def: The Shima region of Mie Prefecture, on the coast of central Japan, one of the three regions whose two-grave villages the Kawazoe survey measured.

hogo.def: A belt of planted trees round a village and its farmland in the Ryukyus, against typhoons and salt wind; the kingdom encouraged them in the eighteenth century, and Tarama's dates to 1742.

Tsugaru.def: The northwestern corner of Japan's main island, in today's Aomori prefecture, and the domain of the Tsugaru lords who ruled it in the Edo period; its western plain takes a salt wind and blown sand off the sea.

Sai On.def: A statesman of the Ryukyu kingdom (1682-1761) who reformed its forestry and had village tree belts, the hogo, planted round its settlements.

principal axis.def: The line through a scatter of points along which they spread widest; of a drawn belt, the direction its clumps run.

centipede lane.def: Pingyao's name for the smallest of its three kinds of street, below its four main streets and eight small streets; seventy-two of them run through the old city, tying together some 4,000 house compounds.

Jin dynasty.def: The dynasty of the Jurchen people that ruled northern China from 1115 to 1234. Its capital, Zhongdu, stood on part of the site of later Beijing.

top-dressing.def: Fertilizer spread on a crop that is already growing, rather than worked into the soil before planting, like the liquid manure a farmer ladles onto rice.

Taiping.def: The Taiping Rebellion (1850-64), an uprising against the Qing that took Nanjing in 1853 and held it as its capital.

finance commissioner.def: An officer of the Tokugawa shogunate over its finances and the revenue of its own lands. Villages near Edo brought petitions to this office.

kengyō.def: The highest rank in the Edo-period guild of blind men, who worked as musicians, masseurs and moneylenders. Written after a personal name as a title.

sexagenary year.def: A year's name in the sixty-year cycle, which pairs one of ten "stems" with one of the twelve zodiac animals. Inscriptions gave it beside the era year.

band.def: The range within which a share or size is rolled - per hamlet or per homestead - so that drawn maps vary inside what the record attests.

Fubokuwakasho.def: A Japanese collection of poems compiled about 1310. The earliest known use of the word itabashi, "plank bridge", is in a poem of its sixteenth book.

Pacific High.def: The large area of high air pressure over the North Pacific that Japan's southeasterly summer wind blows out of - the summer partner of the Siberian High, whose northwesterly wind rules the winter.

canopy-tree.def: A tree with a broad crown of leaves overhead - cedar, oak, zelkova and the like. The maps draw each one as a single crown at its real size, on real spacing; bamboo, whose stems are too thin to see at map scale, is drawn by a convention instead.

1868.def: The year Japan began to modernize: the Meiji Restoration ended the Edo period, and in the decades after it railways, new crops and fertilizers, land reform and new ways of building changed the countryside so much that a survey or photograph from after 1868 is often poor evidence for the landscape before it. That is why the research keeps asking what stood before 1868 - the maps show the countryside as it was before then.

niwa.def: A Japanese farmhouse's work yard - the open ground beside the house where the harvest was threshed and the grain dried on straw mats, commonly measured by the number of mats it held.

fan foot.def: The lower rim of an alluvial fan, where the water that sank into the fan's gravel rises again as springs; settlements often line up along it in an arc.

forest village.def: A village form of northern Germany in which each farm's house stands at the head of its own long strip of field, with woodland at the strip's far end. The Musashino strip rows take the same form.

ressen.def: 列村: a settlement stretched long and thin in a line, its houses along a natural levee, the spring line at a hill's foot, a spring or a waterway, standing on one side of that line or on both. Japanese geography sets it beside the road village (roson), whose line is a road.

shirakashi.def: Shirakashi (シラカシ), a Japanese oak rendered "white oak" - one of the kashi oaks of a tree list - planted with zelkova along a Santome homestead's road side, where the two made an avenue.

dry edge.def: The line where the dry ground a village stands on meets the wet paddy below it. On the map it is the field's margin, standing for a levee, a dike or a fan's foot, and a row village strings its farms along it.

field channel.def: The smallest ditch of the irrigation system, led off a branch ditch to the paddies it waters; the map draws it with a 2.5 ft bed, the narrowest water it draws legibly.

sakuba-michi.def: A field road: a narrow way from a village out to its fields. One Edo-period table of road classes gives it as 3 shaku (about 90 cm) wide.

hundred articles.def: A document of about a hundred instructions on governing, credited to Ieyasu and often called his testament. It exists in several versions, was added to after his death and was partly drafted by his successors.

recension.def: One of several versions of the same text, each revised or edited differently from the others.

cluster's spine.def: A hamlet's main lane, the one the whole settlement walks to its paddy, running through its cluster of farmsteads; the maps draw it one rank wider than a footpath.

provincial abbot.def: In this setting, the cleric that every provincial city keeps at least one of, serving in the city's subordinate temples under the Ministry of Rites. Above them, a domain capital keeps at least two grand abbots.

Ministry of Rites.def: In this setting, the ministry that oversees the shrines and temples and their clergy: the country monks of the village districts, the preceptors of the county towns and the abbots of the cities.

state cult.def: The official worship the Chinese state required of every county seat and city, carried out at its altars, such as the altar to the gods of soil and grain, and at temples such as the City God's.

principal shrine.def: The chief shrine of a Japanese city or province, ranked above the other shrines there.

Amaterasu.def: The sun goddess of Shinto, the chief of its deities, held to be the ancestor of the imperial house; many village shrines enshrine her beside their own god.

Dairokuten.def: A Buddhist deity, the lord of the sixth heaven of the world of desire, enshrined in many small village shrines of the Kanto region in the Edo period.

farmers' stage.def: A stage farmers built, most often on a shrine's grounds, for the kabuki and puppet plays performed in the villages from the eighteenth century on.

talisman.def: A paper charm from a shrine, kept at home on the household's altar shelf.

subsidiary shrine.def: A small shrine standing within a larger shrine's precinct beside its main hall, enshrining a kami connected with the main shrine's own kami or with the shrine itself; in Japanese, sessha and massha.

haibutsu kishaku.def: The purge of Buddhism that followed the 1868 order separating the kami from the Buddhas, in which temples of every kind were torn down - an estimated 30,000 Buddhist structures between 1868 and 1874.

Jinguji Muka.def: As the English encyclopedia names it, the government office that issued the first order separating the kami from the Buddhas, in April 1868.

Jizo-bon.def: A town block's festival for its jizo, centered on children, held chiefly in the Kinki region around Kyoto; a block with no jizo of its own borrows one from a temple or uses a Buddhist painting.

Myojin.def: A title of honor given to a Shinto deity, meaning "bright deity", often joined to the deity's name, as in Wakamiya Myojin.

soja.def: A shrine near a province's capital where all the province's deities were enshrined together, so that their rites could be performed at once.

hall-hermitage.def: A small Buddhist hall, served by a monk or by religionists from the village, without a temple's standing; in the seventeenth century many were raised to temples when their villages became their parishioners.

Dazaifu.def: The old seat of the imperial government's headquarters for Kyushu, near present-day Fukuoka; "the lands under the Dazaifu" are the provinces of Kyushu.

Honzan.def: A line of shugen (mountain asceticism), headed by the temple Shōgoin in Kyoto; a shugen hall "of the Honzan line" was under Shōgoin.

sen.def: A hundredth of a yen, the Meiji money unit between the yen and the rin; a land value in the Saitama temple register is given in yen, sen and rin.

training retreat.def: A set season of concentrated practice for monks in training, which the Sōtō school required its ranked temples to hold; such a temple had to keep a full set of buildings for it - main hall, kuri, meditation hall, dormitory and gate.

kogein.def: Another name for a great house's family temple (bodaiji): the Date house's Zuihoji is called one, where the Tokugawa's Kan'eiji and Zojoji are called bodaiji.

Asuka period.def: An early period of Japanese history, from which clans first built temples of their own (ujidera) - nine centuries before the castle towns.

Benten.def: The Fortune of romantic love, one of the setting's Fortunes.

Jurojin.def: The Fortune of longevity, one of the setting's Fortunes.

Hotei.def: The Fortune of contentment, one of the setting's Fortunes.

Daikoku.def: The Fortune of wealth, one of the setting's Fortunes.

Mahavira hall.def: The main hall of a Chinese Buddhist temple, where its principal image of the Buddha is enshrined; the name calls the Buddha the "great hero."

Vinaya.def: The code of rules that governs Buddhist monks and nuns; a Vinaya house was one devoted to keeping and teaching that discipline, as a Chan house was to meditation.

Ruiju Sandai Kyaku.def: A Heian-period digest of Japan's supplementary laws and edicts, drawn from three earlier compilations of the 9th and early 10th centuries and arranged by subject.

water-and-land hall.def: A hall of a Chinese Buddhist temple for the water-and-land rite, a great service that feeds and frees the souls of all the dead, of water and of land.

shake-machi.def: A quarter of a Japanese town where the houses of a shrine's hereditary priest families gathered near the shrine they served, as at Kamigamo in Kyoto and Takabatake in Nara.

yakudana.def: In the Edo period, the shops on Sensoji's approach nearest the temple, from the Denboin to the Niomon. They were held by local residents whose right to trade there came with the duty of cleaning the temple's precinct and approach.

Kaminarimon.def: The "Thunder Gate," the outer gate of Sensoji in Edo, where its shop-lined approach begins.

Niomon.def: A temple's inner gate, guarded by two fierce guardian statues (Nio). At Sensoji it stands at the temple end of the shop-lined approach.

Denboin.def: The head priest's residence at Sensoji, beside the approach near the Niomon.

Republican era.def: China under the Republic, from the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912 to 1949.

lingxing gate.def: The ceremonial gateway at the front of a Chinese Confucian temple, first on the temple's axis, before the Dacheng gate.

Minglun hall.def: The lecture hall of a Chinese Confucian official school, on the school's own axis beside or behind its temple.

Chongsheng shrine.def: The rear shrine or hall of a Chinese Confucian temple, standing behind its main hall, the Dacheng Hall.

Zunjing pavilion.def: The library pavilion of a Chinese Confucian official school, last on the school's axis.

grand abbot.def: In this setting, the head of one of the Orders across a domain, serving in the Order's sovereign temple in the domain capital; every domain capital keeps at least two, above the provincial abbots of its provincial cities.

state altar.def: In Ming and Qing China, an altar at a seat of local government where the state's own sacrifices were made - to the gods of soil and grain, to wind, clouds, thunder, rain, mountains and rivers, and to the unquiet dead; the gazetteers set each toward its own side of the seat, several outside a gate.

yashiki-baka.def: A household's grave set on its own house land, within the house plot or beside it, rather than at a temple or in a shared graveyard; many households once kept one, and from the Meiji period on many were moved to communal grounds.

katakana.def: One of the two Japanese syllabaries, which spells a word by its sound; a page writing a word in katakana rather than in Chinese characters gives its sound but not its written form.

ribbon-valley.def: A narrow valley whose paddies run as a thin strip along its stream between the slopes on either side; one of the kinds of land a paddy map is drawn on.

bochi.def: Japanese for a graveyard or burial ground: the ground where a settlement, a temple or a household buries its dead.

Nikko Kaido.def: The highway leaving Edo to the north, toward Nikko; the Kozukappara execution ground stood at the city's entrance on it.

Fox Clan.def: A minor clan of the setting, ruled by the Kitsune lineage from the Kitsune forest, with four provincial lineages each administering one of its four provinces; its living comes from the forest, charcoal above all.

sedan.def: A covered chair for one passenger, carried on poles by bearers; in Ming and Qing China the usual way officials and well-off townspeople traveled through a city.

administrative village.def: In Edo-period Japan, the village as a unit of tax and office: it answered jointly for its land tax, and could be one settlement (a natural village) or take in several, more of them in the mountains than on the plain.

Hantei.def: The line of Emperors of Rokugan; each Emperor takes the name and a number in the line, as in "Hantei the Tenth".

Great Clan.def: One of the major clans of Rokugan, each holding its domains under the Emperor. A clan's cities each keep a temple to its two patron Fortunes.

nuisance trade.def: A craft that fouls the air or water around it, such as tanning or dyeing. Our maps place these trades downstream of the drinking water and away from it.

domain.def: The lands one daimyo holds and governs from a capital, divided into provinces, counties and village districts.

branch hamlet.def: A hamlet settled from an older parent village and belonging to it; in Edo-period Japan it usually paid its tax through the parent and had no headman of its own.

ie.def: The Japanese household as a continuing house: its family, dwelling, land and name, handed on each generation from the head to one married heir.

genin.def: A bound servant of a farm household in early Edo-period Japan, who worked the master's land and often lived on the master's house plot; over the period most became independent small farmers.

collateral kin.def: Relatives outside the direct line of descent, such as a head's brothers, their wives and children, or cousins, living in the head's household.

headland.def: An unplanted strip at the edge of a field; on our maps, the strip along the drain at the narrow end of a fan of paddies, where a point too sharp to level and plant is cut off.

half-fold.def: One of the ways the ancient jori grid divided a square of one cho into ten one-tan paddies: each plot 30 by 12 ken, laid in two rows of five.

nagachi.def: The long-strip way of dividing a jori grid's square unit (tsubo) into its ten tan: ten long, narrow strips, each running the full length of the square.

hanori.def: The half-fold way of dividing a jori grid's square unit (tsubo) into its ten tan: the square is cut in half, and each half is cut into five strips.

extensive agriculture.def: Farming that spreads its work thinly over much land, leaving some ground to rest and choosing each year which plots to crop, as the early medieval estates did where water or soil could not carry every plot every year. The opposite of intensive farming.

intensive farming.def: Farming that crops the same stable land every year and puts more labor into each plot, as the nucleated villages came to do. The opposite of extensive agriculture.

Kagawa.def: A prefecture of Shikoku on the Seto Inland Sea, taking in the Sanuki plain. It has the most irrigation ponds for its area of any prefecture in Japan, and before its canal opened, ponds supplied most of its farm water.

San'yo.def: The region along the Seto Inland Sea's northern shore, west of Kinki. It gets little rain, and like Shikoku it depends on irrigation ponds.

raised-bed river.def: A river whose bed has built up with gravel between fixed banks until it runs higher than the land around it.

hill spacing.def: In rice planting, the distance between hills, the clumps of seedlings set into the paddy together at one spot. Today it is about 30 cm; before the Meiji period the clumps were set by eye, in no even rows.

Kofu.def: A basin in Kai province, today's Yamanashi, west of the Kanto plain. Its floor is built of alluvial fans, and they were cleared early.

rapeseed cake.def: The pressed residue left after the oil is squeezed from rapeseed, sold to farmers as a fertilizer.

kiku.def: Japanese for the chrysanthemum. It came to Japan from China as a medicine and an ornament, became the emblem of the imperial house, and was bred into many distinct lines in the Edo period.

araizeki.def: A weir built to let the water run over its crest at all times, not only in flood. With the grass weir, one of the two kinds an official handbook sorts the Edo-period farm weirs into.

grass weir.def: A simple weir of stakes driven into a stream with reed (kaya) woven between them, used where a permanent weir is not allowed. One is still built today at Chiyoda, in Saga.

Zhengguo canal.def: An ancient Chinese irrigation canal of the third century BC; scholars disagree whether its head had a dam across the river or took the water off a bend without one.

Asakura period.def: The century, about 1471 to 1573, when the Asakura warrior house ruled Echizen province from its castle town at Ichijodani.

land fall.def: The direction a map's ground slopes downhill, which every map declares because no contour lines draw it; given in degrees turning clockwise from east, so 90 is south.

drainage bearing.def: The direction a map's water leaves it, declared beside the land fall and given in the same degrees, turning clockwise from east.

Hattori site.def: An excavated archaeological site of early Yayoi-period paddy fields, where the widths and heights of both the large bunds along the canals and the small bunds between plots were measured.

percolation.def: Water soaking down through the floor of a paddy into the ground below. It is lost to the field, and more is lost when the groundwater level falls.

lined canal.def: A canal whose bed and banks are faced with concrete, stone or another hard surface, unlike a ditch dug in the bare earth.

bunsui.def: Dividing one channel's water between two or more channels, areas or villages - by rules fixing each channel's width, its gate hours and the turns it took, or by a built work at the fork such as a graduated stake, a proportional flume or a round divider.

cylinder divider.def: A round concrete work that splits a canal's flow between channels in exact proportion. It is a modern device: the first was built in 1914, long after the period our maps are set in.

division flume.def: A built work set across a fork in a ditch or canal that divides its water among the branches in fixed shares, as at Kuji in the mid-Edo period, where the shares followed the cultivated area each branch watered.

suisha.def: A water wheel (水車), and the water mill it drove: in Edo-period Japan a wheel turned by a stream that worked pestles pounding rice in mortars, or millstones grinding grain. Most were owned by wealthy farmers or village officials.

mizubune.def: A spring-fed washing tank at Gujo Hachiman: water from a spring or a valley is piped into a tank of two or three tiers, the top for drinking, the middle for rinsing food, and the bottom for dirty things and the mud off vegetables.

segi-ita.def: A board slotted into a groove in a channel or small stream to hold the water back for a while: used most for daily washing, and also for sprinkling in summer, melting snow in winter, and splitting the flow.

shitchi.def: Japanese for marsh or wetland: low ground where water stands or the soil stays wet, the reed ground that wet rice was reclaimed from and that stayed reed wherever draining stopped.

mere.def: A shallow lake or pond of standing water; a Northern Song official proposed joining meres, marshes and dikes into a belt across the northern frontier to hold back an enemy's cavalry.

military farm colony.def: A frontier settlement where soldiers farmed the land they guarded, so the garrison fed itself; a Song proposal would have watered such colonies from a belt of meres and dikes against cavalry.

secondary succession.def: Wild plants returning to ground that was cleared and then let go, one plant community giving way to the next with no one planting them; on an abandoned paddy, annual weeds come first, then knotweed, then sedge.

Home Ministry.def: The ministry of Japan's Meiji government in charge of domestic affairs; in 1884 it issued the rules for siting new graveyards.

ox-bow lake.def: A curved lake left on a river plain where a bend of the river has been cut off from its channel.

endorheic.def: Of a basin or lake: having no outlet to the sea, so that its water leaves only by evaporation and seepage; such basins are found most often in deserts.

Jowa.def: A Japanese era name; its second year, Jowa 2, is the year 835.

Crab Clan.def: A Great Clan of the setting, which holds the empire's most dangerous border, against the Shadowlands; its lands have rich iron deposits and good land for growing tea.

diluvial upland.def: Raised, fairly flat ground of older river or sea deposits standing above today's alluvial plain - in Japan the plateaus beside the lowlands, drier than the plain and harder to bring water to, so long left as upland fields or woods.

fry.def: Young fish newly hatched, raised in nursery ponds and sold to stock other ponds; Jiujiang township in the Pearl River delta lived largely by the trade in them.

people's commune.def: In the People's Republic of China from 1958 into the early 1980s, the unit of collective farming and local government that grouped a number of villages.

modern times.def: In this record, the years after the old order ended: in China after its last dynasty, the Qing, fell in 1912, and in Japan after 1868. A form found only in modern times is left off the maps.

Qu Dajun.def: A seventeenth-century Cantonese scholar whose account of Guangdong, the Guangdong xinyu, completed in 1678, is the oldest description of the Pearl River delta's pond dikes this record has read.
